name: Skull
location: Head; sits on the first cervical vertebra (atlas).
description: The bony framework of the head, made up of the cranial bones that enclose the brain and the facial bones that form the face.
function: Protects the brain and special sense organs, supports the face and provides attachment for muscles of mastication and facial expression.
clinicalRelevance: The pterion is a thin region of the lateral skull; fracture here can tear the underlying middle meningeal artery and cause an extradural (epidural) haematoma.
learningObjectives: Identify the foramen magnum and its contents

name: Vertebral column
location: Posterior midline from the skull to the pelvis.
description: A flexible column of vertebrae: typically 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. Intervertebral discs separate adjacent vertebral bodies.
function: Supports the head and trunk, protects the spinal cord, allows movement of the trunk and transmits body weight to the pelvis.
clinicalRelevance: Herniation of an intervertebral disc can compress an adjacent spinal nerve root, producing pain and sensory or motor changes in its distribution.
learningObjectives: State the number of vertebrae in each region
Explain the protective relationship between vertebrae and the spinal cord

name: Sternum
location: Anterior midline of the thorax.
description: A flat bone made of three parts: the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.
function: Forms the anterior thoracic wall, protects the heart and great vessels and anchors the clavicles and costal cartilages.
articulations: Costal cartilages of the true ribs
clinicalRelevance: The sternal angle lies level with the second costal cartilage and is used as a landmark for counting ribs and intercostal spaces during clinical examination.

name: Ribs
location: Thoracic wall, extending from the thoracic vertebrae towards the sternum.
description: Twelve pairs of curved bones. Ribs 1–7 are true ribs (costal cartilages attach directly to the sternum); ribs 8–12 are false ribs, of which 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no anterior attachment.
function: Protect thoracic and upper abdominal organs and move during breathing to change thoracic volume.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures of the lower left ribs can injure the underlying spleen.

name: Clavicle
location: Horizontally across the root of the neck, from the sternum to the scapula.
description: An S-shaped bone that forms the anterior part of the shoulder (pectoral) girdle.
function: Acts as a strut holding the upper limb away from the trunk and transmits forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
clinicalRelevance: One of the most commonly fractured bones, typically after a fall onto the shoulder or outstretched hand.

name: Scapula
location: Posterolateral thoracic wall.
description: A flat, triangular bone that forms the posterior part of the shoulder girdle.
function: Provides the socket of the shoulder joint and attachment for muscles that move the shoulder and arm.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures are uncommon and mean a high-energy injury. Winging of the scapula follows injury to the long thoracic nerve. Shoulder impingement under the acromion is common.

name: Humerus
location: Arm, between the shoulder and elbow.
description: The single long bone of the arm.
function: Transmits forces between shoulder and elbow and provides attachment for muscles that move the shoulder and elbow.
clinicalRelevance: Nerves lie close to the bone: the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the radial groove of the shaft and the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle. Fractures at these sites can injure the related nerve.

name: Radius
location: Lateral (thumb side) forearm.
description: The lateral bone of the forearm, narrow at the elbow and broad at the wrist.
function: Rotates around the ulna during pronation and supination and forms the main forearm contribution to the wrist joint.
clinicalRelevance: A fracture of the distal radius is a common injury after a fall on an outstretched hand.

name: Ulna
location: Medial (little-finger side) forearm.
description: The medial bone of the forearm, large at the elbow and narrow at the wrist.
function: Forms the main hinge of the elbow joint with the trochlea of the humerus.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures of the shaft (nightstick fracture) and the olecranon, and the Monteggia fracture-dislocation. The ulnar nerve can be squeezed at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome).

name: Hip bone
location: Pelvis; the two hip bones and the sacrum form the bony pelvis.
description: Each hip bone forms from three bones — ilium, ischium and pubis — which fuse at the acetabulum.
function: Transfers body weight from the vertebral column to the lower limbs and supports pelvic organs.
clinicalRelevance: Pelvic fractures after trauma can bleed heavily. Hip dysplasia and femoroacetabular impingement affect the socket (acetabulum).

name: Femur
location: Thigh, between the hip and knee.
description: The longest and strongest bone in the body.
articulations: Hip bone (hip joint, at the acetabulum)
function: Bears body weight and acts as a lever for muscles of the hip and knee.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures of the femoral neck, common in older adults, can disrupt the blood supply to the femoral head and lead to avascular necrosis.
learningObjectives: Identify the major landmarks of the femur
Explain why femoral neck fractures can threaten the femoral head

name: Patella
location: Anterior knee, within the quadriceps tendon.
description: The largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps femoris.
function: Protects the knee joint and improves the leverage of the quadriceps femoris.
clinicalRelevance: Dislocation, fracture after a fall on the knee, patellofemoral pain and chondromalacia (softening of the cartilage under the kneecap).

name: Tibia
location: Medial leg.
description: The larger, weight-bearing bone of the leg.
function: Transmits body weight from the femur to the foot.
clinicalRelevance: The commonest long bone fracture; it can cause compartment syndrome. Also shin splints, plateau fractures at the knee and bone infection (osteomyelitis).

name: Fibula
location: Lateral leg.
description: A slender bone lateral to the tibia that carries little body weight.
function: Provides muscle attachment and stabilises the ankle via the lateral malleolus.
clinicalRelevance: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it can be injured by fracture or pressure, causing foot drop.

name: Deltoid
location: Forms the rounded contour of the shoulder.
description: A thick, triangular muscle covering the shoulder joint, with anterior, middle and posterior parts.
origin: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula.
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.
actions: Middle fibres abduct the arm; anterior fibres flex and medially rotate it; posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate it.
clinicalRelevance: Injury to the axillary nerve (for example with a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus) weakens abduction and can cause numbness over the lower deltoid.

name: Biceps brachii
location: Anterior compartment of the arm.
description: A two-headed muscle of the anterior arm.
origin: Short head: tip of the coracoid process of the scapula. Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.
insertion: Radial tuberosity and, via the bicipital aponeurosis, the deep fascia of the forearm.
actions: Flexes the elbow and is a powerful supinator of the forearm; also assists flexion of the shoulder.
clinicalRelevance: The biceps tendon reflex tests the C5–C6 spinal segments.

name: Triceps brachii
location: Posterior compartment of the arm.
description: A three-headed muscle forming the bulk of the posterior arm.
origin: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula. Lateral and medial heads: posterior surface of the humerus, above and below the radial groove respectively.
insertion: Olecranon of the ulna.
actions: Extends the elbow; the long head also helps extend the shoulder.
clinicalRelevance: Tendon rupture is rare. Radial nerve injury paralyses it. The triceps reflex tests the C7 nerve root.

name: Pectoralis major
location: Anterior chest wall.
description: A large, fan-shaped muscle with clavicular and sternocostal heads.
origin: Clavicular head: medial half of the clavicle. Sternocostal head: sternum and upper costal cartilages.
insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
actions: Adducts and medially rotates the arm; the clavicular head also flexes the arm.
clinicalRelevance: Rupture during weightlifting, strain, and congenital absence in Poland syndrome.

name: Rectus abdominis
location: Anterior abdominal wall, either side of the midline (linea alba).
description: A long, strap-like muscle divided by tendinous intersections and enclosed in the rectus sheath.
origin: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis.
insertion: Xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5–7.
innervation: Anterior rami of the lower thoracic spinal nerves (thoraco-abdominal and subcostal nerves).
actions: Flexes the trunk and compresses the abdominal contents.
clinicalRelevance: Diastasis recti (the two halves separate) after pregnancy, hernias through the midline, and muscle strains.

name: Diaphragm
location: Dome-shaped partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
description: A musculotendinous sheet whose peripheral muscle fibres converge on a central tendon.
origin: Xiphoid process, inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs, and the upper lumbar vertebrae (via the crura).
insertion: Central tendon.
actions: The principal muscle of inspiration: contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume.
clinicalRelevance: Because the phrenic nerve arises from C3–C5, high cervical spinal cord injuries can impair breathing. Irritation of the diaphragm can be felt as pain referred to the shoulder region.
learningObjectives: State the motor nerve supply of the diaphragm
Explain the role of the diaphragm in quiet inspiration

name: Rectus femoris
location: Anterior compartment of the thigh; one of the four parts of quadriceps femoris.
description: The only part of quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip joint.
origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head) and the ilium just above the acetabulum (reflected head).
insertion: Base of the patella via the quadriceps tendon, and onward to the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament.
actions: Extends the knee and flexes the hip.
clinicalRelevance: Tapping the patellar ligament (knee-jerk reflex) tests the femoral nerve and the L3–L4 segments.

name: Gastrocnemius
location: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg (calf).
description: A two-headed superficial calf muscle.
origin: Medial head: above the medial femoral condyle. Lateral head: lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle.
insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
actions: Plantar flexes the foot at the ankle and helps flex the knee.
clinicalRelevance: The ankle-jerk reflex tests the S1 segment through the calcaneal tendon.

name: Heart
location: Middle mediastinum, behind the sternum, with its apex pointing down, forward and to the left.
description: A four-chambered muscular pump enclosed in the pericardium.
function: The right side pumps blood through the pulmonary circulation; the left side pumps blood through the systemic circulation.
bloodSupply: Right and left coronary arteries, arising from the ascending aorta.
venousDrainage: Mainly cardiac veins draining to the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium.
clinicalRelevance: Blockage of a coronary artery reduces blood flow to the region of myocardium it supplies (myocardial ischaemia or infarction).
learningObjectives: Name the four chambers of the heart
Trace blood through the heart in order

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Right atrium
location: Right border of the heart.
description: The chamber that receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body.
function: Receives blood from the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle. Contains the sinoatrial (SA) node, the normal pacemaker.
clinicalRelevance: Atrial fibrillation and flutter, atrial septal defects, and enlargement in tricuspid valve disease.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Right ventricle
location: Forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart.
description: The chamber that pumps blood to the lungs.
function: Pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
clinicalRelevance: Right heart failure (cor pulmonale) from lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and tetralogy of Fallot.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Left atrium
location: Forms most of the base (posterior surface) of the heart.
description: The chamber that receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
function: Receives blood from the pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.
clinicalRelevance: The left atrium lies directly in front of the oesophagus, which is why it can be imaged by transoesophageal echocardiography.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Left ventricle
location: Forms the apex and most of the left border of the heart.
description: The chamber with the thickest muscular wall.
function: Pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and systemic circulation, against much higher pressure than the right ventricle.
clinicalRelevance: Heart attack (myocardial infarction), heart failure, thickening (hypertrophy) from high blood pressure or aortic stenosis, and cardiomyopathy.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Tricuspid valve
location: Between the right atrium and right ventricle.
description: An atrioventricular valve with three cusps, anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles.
function: Prevents backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium during ventricular contraction.
clinicalRelevance: Regurgitation (endocarditis in people who inject drugs, Ebstein anomaly) and stenosis. It causes swollen neck veins and leg swelling.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Pulmonary valve
location: Between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.
description: A semilunar valve with three cusps.
function: Prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle.
clinicalRelevance: Congenital stenosis, and regurgitation after repair of tetralogy of Fallot.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Mitral valve
location: Between the left atrium and left ventricle.
description: An atrioventricular valve with two cusps, anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles.
function: Prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular contraction.
clinicalRelevance: Stenosis (usually from rheumatic fever), regurgitation and prolapse. They lead to breathlessness and atrial fibrillation.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Aortic valve
location: Between the left ventricle and the ascending aorta.
description: A semilunar valve with three cusps.
function: Prevents backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle.
clinicalRelevance: Aortic stenosis (calcification in older adults or a bicuspid valve) causes chest pain, fainting and breathlessness. Regurgitation causes a large pulse pressure.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Coronary arteries
location: On the surface of the heart, arising from the root of the ascending aorta.
description: The right and left coronary arteries and their branches. The left coronary artery typically divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) and circumflex branches.
function: Supply oxygenated blood to the myocardium.
clinicalRelevance: Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries is the basis of coronary artery disease.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Pulmonary veins
location: From the hilum of each lung to the posterior wall of the left atrium.
description: Usually four veins, two from each lung, that carry blood away from the lungs.
function: Return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, completing the pulmonary circulation.
clinicalRelevance: Unlike most veins, the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood — a common point tested in exams.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Cardiac veins
location: On the surface of the heart, mainly in the coronary and interventricular sulci.
description: Veins of the heart wall, including the great, middle and small cardiac veins. Most join the coronary sinus on the posterior surface of the heart.
function: Drain deoxygenated blood from the myocardium; the coronary sinus empties into the right atrium.
clinicalRelevance: The coronary sinus is used for pacing leads in cardiac resynchronisation. A persistent left superior vena cava drains into it.

sources.locator: Chapter 19: The Cardiovascular System: The Heart

name: Aorta
location: Arises from the left ventricle, arches over the root of the left lung and descends through the thorax and abdomen.
description: The largest artery, described as the ascending aorta, aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta.
function: Distributes oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. Branches of the arch are the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery.
clinicalRelevance: The abdominal aorta divides into the right and left common iliac arteries at about the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra. Abnormal dilation of the aorta is called an aneurysm.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Pulmonary trunk
location: Arises from the right ventricle anterior to the ascending aorta.
description: A short, wide vessel that divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
function: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle towards the lungs.
clinicalRelevance: Pulmonary embolism blocks its branches, pulmonary hypertension widens it, and a patent ductus arteriosus joins it.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superior vena cava
location: Right side of the superior mediastinum, ending in the right atrium.
description: A large vein formed by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins.
function: Returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and upper thorax to the right atrium.
clinicalRelevance: Superior vena cava syndrome from lung cancer or lymphoma causes swelling of the face and arms. Thrombosis around central lines.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Inferior vena cava
location: Ascends on the right of the abdominal aorta, passes through the diaphragm and ends in the right atrium.
description: The largest vein, formed by the union of the common iliac veins.
function: Returns deoxygenated blood from the lower limbs, pelvis and abdomen to the right atrium.
clinicalRelevance: Compression by the womb in late pregnancy causes low blood pressure when lying on the back. Clot filters, and tumour growth into it (for example renal cell carcinoma).

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Common carotid artery
location: Ascends in the neck within the carotid sheath. The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left arises directly from the aortic arch.
description: A major artery of the neck that divides into the internal and external carotid arteries.
function: Supplies blood to the head and neck; the internal carotid artery is a major supply to the brain.
clinicalRelevance: The carotid pulse can be felt in the neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Brachial artery
location: Medial arm, continuing to the cubital fossa where it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
description: The continuation of the axillary artery in the arm.
function: The main arterial supply of the arm.
clinicalRelevance: Its pulse is palpated in the cubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon, when measuring blood pressure with a cuff.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Common iliac artery
location: From the aortic bifurcation to the pelvic brim, on each side.
description: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta. Each divides into internal and external iliac arteries.
function: Supplies the pelvis and, through the external iliac artery, the lower limb.
clinicalRelevance: Atherosclerosis and aneurysm. Blockage causes pain in the buttock and legs on walking (claudication), and Leriche syndrome.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Femoral artery
location: Anterior and medial thigh, beginning in the femoral triangle.
description: The continuation of the external iliac artery after it passes beneath the inguinal ligament.
function: The main arterial supply of the lower limb.
clinicalRelevance: Its pulse can be felt just below the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The artery is commonly used for vascular access.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Brain
location: Cranial cavity.
description: The part of the central nervous system within the skull, comprising the cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum.
function: Integrates sensory information, generates movement, and supports cognition, emotion and homeostatic control.
bloodSupply: Internal carotid and vertebral arteries, which connect around the cerebral arterial circle (circle of Willis).
clinicalRelevance: Stroke, dementia (including Alzheimer disease), brain tumours, epilepsy, Parkinson disease, head injury and meningitis.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Cerebrum
location: Occupies most of the cranial cavity.
description: The two cerebral hemispheres, each divided into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, with an outer layer of grey matter (cerebral cortex).
function: Higher functions including voluntary movement, conscious sensation, language, memory and reasoning.
clinicalRelevance: Stroke, epilepsy, tumours and dementia. Damage to each lobe gives its own deficit, for example language loss (aphasia), neglect or loss of vision.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Cerebellum
location: Posterior cranial fossa, behind the brainstem and below the occipital lobes.
description: A highly folded structure attached to the brainstem.
function: Coordinates movement, posture and balance and contributes to motor learning.
clinicalRelevance: Damage to one cerebellar hemisphere typically produces incoordination (ataxia) on the same side of the body.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Brainstem
location: Connects the cerebrum and diencephalon to the spinal cord.
description: Comprises the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.
function: Conducts tracts between brain and spinal cord, contains nuclei of most cranial nerves and houses centres that regulate breathing and cardiovascular function.
clinicalRelevance: Brainstem stroke (can cause locked-in syndrome), herniation causing coma and death, and multiple sclerosis. It controls breathing and heartbeat.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Spinal cord
location: Vertebral canal, from the foramen magnum to about the level of the L1–L2 vertebrae in adults.
description: A cylindrical part of the central nervous system giving rise to 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Below its tapered end (conus medullaris) the vertebral canal contains the nerve roots of the cauda equina.
function: Conducts sensory and motor signals between the body and the brain and mediates spinal reflexes.
clinicalRelevance: Because the adult cord usually ends around L1–L2, lumbar puncture is performed below this level, commonly at L3–L4 or L4–L5.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Brachial plexus
location: From the root of the neck, passing behind the clavicle into the axilla.
description: A network formed by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C5–T1, organised into roots, trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches.
function: Supplies motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb. Terminal branches include the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.
clinicalRelevance: Traction injuries to the upper roots (C5–C6) produce a characteristic upper-limb posture known as Erb palsy.

name: Axillary nerve
location: Passes around the surgical neck of the humerus.
description: A branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5, C6).
function: Supplies the deltoid and teres minor and the skin over the lower deltoid.
clinicalRelevance: Injured by shoulder dislocation or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus: deltoid weakness and a patch of numbness over the shoulder.

name: Musculocutaneous nerve
location: Anterior compartment of the arm.
description: A terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.
function: Supplies the muscles of the anterior arm, including biceps brachii, and skin of the lateral forearm.
clinicalRelevance: Injury weakens bending of the elbow and turning the palm up, with numbness of the outer forearm. It can be hurt in shoulder injuries or surgery.

name: Radial nerve
location: Runs in the radial groove on the posterior humerus, then passes anterior to the lateral epicondyle into the forearm.
description: A terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.
function: Supplies the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm, including triceps brachii, and skin of the posterior arm, forearm and part of the hand.
clinicalRelevance: Injury in the radial groove (for example with a mid-shaft humeral fracture) can cause wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist extensors.

name: Phrenic nerve
location: Descends through the neck and thorax, passing anterior to the root of the lung, to reach the diaphragm.
description: A nerve arising mainly from the C3–C5 anterior rami of the cervical plexus.
function: Provides the motor supply to the diaphragm.
clinicalRelevance: Injury paralyses half of the diaphragm (it rises on a chest x-ray); causes include neck or chest surgery and lung cancer. Irritation of the diaphragm gives pain at the tip of the shoulder, and hiccups.

name: Vagus nerve
location: Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, descends in the carotid sheath and continues into the thorax and abdomen.
description: The tenth cranial nerve, with a very wide distribution.
function: Carries parasympathetic fibres to thoracic and abdominal viscera (including the heart, lungs and much of the gut), motor fibres to the pharynx and larynx, and sensory fibres from these regions.
clinicalRelevance: Vasovagal fainting, vocal cord paralysis after injury to its recurrent laryngeal branch (thyroid surgery) and delayed stomach emptying (gastroparesis).

name: Femoral nerve
location: Enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery.
description: A branch of the lumbar plexus (L2–L4).
function: Supplies the anterior thigh muscles, including quadriceps femoris, and skin of the anterior thigh and medial leg.
clinicalRelevance: Injury in pelvic surgery, diabetes or a groin bleed weakens knee extension, with numbness of the front of the thigh and inner leg and a lost knee jerk.

name: Sciatic nerve
location: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and descends in the posterior thigh.
description: The largest nerve in the body, formed from the L4–S3 anterior rami of the sacral plexus. It usually divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves above the knee.
function: Supplies the posterior thigh muscles and, through its branches, all muscles below the knee.
clinicalRelevance: Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve.

name: Tibial nerve
location: Popliteal fossa and posterior leg.
description: One of the two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve.
function: Supplies the muscles of the posterior leg, including gastrocnemius, and the sole of the foot.
clinicalRelevance: Tarsal tunnel syndrome at the ankle. Injury weakens pointing the foot down and causes numbness of the sole.

name: Common fibular nerve
location: Winds around the neck of the fibula.
description: One of the two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve.
function: Through its superficial and deep branches, supplies muscles of the lateral and anterior leg, which evert the foot and dorsiflex the ankle.
clinicalRelevance: Injury at the fibular neck causes foot drop.

name: Nasal cavity
location: Behind the external nose, above the hard palate.
description: Paired air passages separated by the nasal septum, with conchae projecting from the lateral walls.
function: Warms, humidifies and filters inspired air and contains the olfactory epithelium.
clinicalRelevance: Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, nosebleeds (epistaxis), a deviated septum and nasal polyps.

name: Pharynx
location: Behind the nasal cavity, oral cavity and larynx.
description: A muscular tube divided into nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx.
function: A shared passage for air and food.
clinicalRelevance: Pharyngitis and tonsillitis, obstructive sleep apnoea, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and nasopharyngeal cancer.

name: Larynx
location: Anterior neck, between the pharynx and trachea.
description: A cartilaginous airway structure including the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage and epiglottis.
function: Conducts air, protects the lower airway during swallowing and produces voice via the vocal folds.
clinicalRelevance: Laryngitis, croup and epiglottitis, vocal cord nodules or paralysis, laryngeal cancer (mostly in smokers) and airway obstruction.

name: Trachea
location: From the larynx through the neck into the superior mediastinum, ending at the carina.
description: An airway held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, completed posteriorly by smooth muscle (trachealis).
function: Conducts air between the larynx and the main bronchi.
clinicalRelevance: The trachea divides into the main bronchi at about the level of the sternal angle.

name: Right main bronchus
location: From the carina to the hilum of the right lung.
description: Wider, shorter and more vertical than the left main bronchus.
function: Conducts air into the right lung.
clinicalRelevance: Because of its shape, an inhaled foreign body is more likely to enter the right main bronchus.

name: Left main bronchus
location: From the carina to the hilum of the left lung, passing below the aortic arch.
description: Narrower, longer and more horizontal than the right main bronchus.
function: Conducts air into the left lung.
clinicalRelevance: It is narrower and more horizontal than the right, so inhaled objects go right more often. Lung cancer or enlarged lymph nodes at the carina can narrow it.

name: Right lung
location: Right pleural cavity.
description: Divided by the oblique and horizontal fissures into three lobes: superior, middle and inferior.
function: Site of gas exchange between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.
clinicalRelevance: Pneumonia, tuberculosis, lung cancer, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, COPD and asthma. Inhaled objects and aspirated fluid pass more often into the right lung.

name: Left lung
location: Left pleural cavity.
description: Divided by the oblique fissure into two lobes: superior and inferior. Its anterior border has a cardiac notch, and the superior lobe has a tongue-like lingula.
function: Site of gas exchange between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.
clinicalRelevance: Pneumonia, lung cancer, pneumothorax, COPD and asthma. Fluid from heart failure collects in both lungs.

name: Alveoli
location: Throughout both lungs, at the ends of the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
description: Tiny, thin-walled air sacs clustered at the end of the respiratory tree. Their walls are lined mainly by type I alveolar cells, with type II alveolar cells and alveolar macrophages, and are surrounded by a dense network of pulmonary capillaries.
function: The site of gas exchange: oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into the capillary blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, across the thin respiratory membrane. Type II cells secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and helps keep alveoli from collapsing.
clinicalRelevance: Premature infants may lack sufficient surfactant, which can cause respiratory distress because alveoli tend to collapse.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of the respiratory membrane

name: Pleura
location: Lines each half of the thoracic cavity and covers each lung.
description: A serous membrane with a visceral layer on the lung surface and a parietal layer lining the thoracic wall, separated by a thin pleural cavity containing fluid.
function: Reduces friction during breathing and couples the lungs to the chest wall.
clinicalRelevance: Air in the pleural cavity (pneumothorax) can cause the lung to collapse.

name: Oral cavity
location: Bounded by the lips, cheeks, palate and floor of the mouth.
description: Contains the teeth and tongue and receives saliva from the salivary glands.
function: Ingestion, mechanical digestion (chewing) and the start of chemical digestion.
clinicalRelevance: Dental caries, gum disease, oral thrush, mouth ulcers and oral cancer (tobacco and alcohol).

name: Oesophagus
location: From the pharynx through the posterior mediastinum, passing through the diaphragm to the stomach.
description: A muscular tube lying behind the trachea and the left atrium.
function: Transports swallowed food to the stomach by peristalsis.
clinicalRelevance: Acid reflux (GORD) and Barrett oesophagus, oesophageal cancer, varices in liver disease, achalasia and strictures.

name: Stomach
location: Left upper abdomen, below the diaphragm.
description: A J-shaped dilated part of the gut with regions called the cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part.
function: Stores food, mixes it with gastric juice containing acid and enzymes, and releases chyme into the duodenum.
clinicalRelevance: Peptic ulcers (H. pylori, anti-inflammatory drugs), gastritis, stomach cancer, reflux and delayed emptying.

name: Liver
location: Right upper abdomen, under the diaphragm and largely protected by the lower ribs.
description: The largest gland in the body.
function: Produces bile and performs many metabolic functions, including processing absorbed nutrients, storing glycogen, synthesising plasma proteins and detoxifying substances.
bloodSupply: Dual supply: the hepatic artery proper (oxygenated blood) and the hepatic portal vein (nutrient-rich blood from the gut).
venousDrainage: Hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava.
clinicalRelevance: Hepatitis, fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, liver cancer and jaundice.

name: Gallbladder
location: In a fossa on the inferior surface of the liver.
description: A small, pear-shaped sac.
function: Stores and concentrates bile and releases it into the duodenum.
clinicalRelevance: Gallstones, cholecystitis (inflammation) and biliary colic. Cancer is rare.

name: Pancreas
location: Posterior to the stomach; mostly retroperitoneal, with its head in the curve of the duodenum.
description: A gland with both exocrine and endocrine tissue.
function: Exocrine acini secrete digestive enzymes into the duodenum; endocrine pancreatic islets secrete hormones including insulin and glucagon.
clinicalRelevance: Pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, diabetes mellitus and cystic fibrosis.

name: Small intestine
location: Central and lower abdomen, from the pylorus to the ileocaecal junction.
description: The longest part of the alimentary canal, divided into duodenum, jejunum and ileum. Its surface area is greatly increased by circular folds, villi and microvilli.
function: Completes chemical digestion and absorbs most nutrients.
clinicalRelevance: Coeliac disease, Crohn disease, duodenal ulcers and bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernias).

name: Large intestine
location: Frames the small intestine around the abdomen, from the caecum to the anal canal.
description: Comprises the caecum (with the appendix), ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal.
function: Absorbs water and electrolytes and forms and stores faeces.
clinicalRelevance: Colorectal cancer, ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis, irritable bowel syndrome and appendicitis.

name: Rectum
location: Pelvis, continuing from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.
description: The terminal part of the large intestine, between the sigmoid colon and the anal canal. Despite its name ("straight"), it follows the curve of the sacrum.
function: Stores faeces before defecation.
clinicalRelevance: Haemorrhoids, anal fissures, rectal cancer and rectal prolapse.

name: Kidney
location: Retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall, roughly between T12 and L3. The right kidney usually lies slightly lower than the left because of the liver.
description: A bean-shaped organ with an outer cortex and inner medulla. Its functional unit is the nephron.
function: Filters blood to form urine, regulates fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance, and produces hormones such as erythropoietin and renin.
bloodSupply: Renal artery from the abdominal aorta.
venousDrainage: Renal vein to the inferior vena cava.
clinicalRelevance: Kidney stones, urinary infection and pyelonephritis, chronic kidney disease, glomerulonephritis and tumours.

name: Ureter
location: From the renal pelvis down the posterior abdominal wall, crossing the pelvic brim, to the bladder.
description: A narrow muscular tube.
function: Transports urine from the kidney to the bladder by peristalsis.
clinicalRelevance: Kidney stones tend to lodge at natural narrowings: the pelvi-ureteric junction, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, and where it enters the bladder wall.

name: Urinary bladder
location: Pelvic cavity, behind the pubic symphysis.
description: A distensible muscular sac whose wall contains the detrusor muscle.
function: Stores urine and expels it during micturition.
clinicalRelevance: Cystitis, bladder cancer, bladder stones, urinary retention (for example with an enlarged prostate) and incontinence.

name: Urethra
location: From the bladder neck to the external urethral orifice.
description: A tube that is considerably longer in males than in females.
function: Conveys urine out of the body; in males it also conveys semen.
clinicalRelevance: Urethritis, strictures, injury in pelvic fractures and hypospadias.

name: Testis
location: Within the scrotum.
description: The male gonad, containing seminiferous tubules and interstitial (Leydig) cells.
function: Produces sperm and secretes testosterone.
clinicalRelevance: The testes develop on the posterior abdominal wall and descend into the scrotum; for this reason testicular lymph drains to lumbar (para-aortic) nodes.

name: Epididymis
location: Along the posterior border of each testis, with a head, body and tail.
description: A tightly coiled duct about 6 m long when uncoiled, packed into a comma-shaped structure.
function: Stores sperm and is where they mature and gain the ability to move.
clinicalRelevance: Epididymitis causes a tender, swollen epididymis and must be distinguished from testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency.

name: Spermatic cord
location: From the deep inguinal ring, through the inguinal canal, to the back of the testis.
description: A bundle containing the ductus (vas) deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform venous plexus, nerves and lymphatics.
function: Carries sperm away from the testis and supplies it with blood.
clinicalRelevance: Twisting of the cord (testicular torsion) cuts off the blood supply; a dilated pampiniform plexus is a varicocele.

name: Scrotum
location: Below the penis, between the thighs.
description: A skin and smooth-muscle (dartos) sac divided by a septum into two compartments, one for each testis.
function: Keeps the testes about 2–3 °C below core body temperature, which sperm production needs.
clinicalRelevance: Hydrocele, varicocele, testicular torsion (an emergency), epididymitis and inguinal hernia.

name: Ovary
location: Lateral pelvic wall, on either side of the uterus.
description: The female gonad, containing ovarian follicles.
function: Produces oocytes and secretes oestrogens and progesterone.
clinicalRelevance: Ovarian cysts, polycystic ovary syndrome, ovarian cancer, torsion and endometriosis.

name: Uterus
location: Pelvic cavity, between the bladder and rectum.
description: A thick-walled muscular organ with a fundus, body and cervix; its wall comprises endometrium, myometrium and perimetrium.
function: Site of implantation and development of the embryo and fetus.
clinicalRelevance: Fibroids, endometriosis, endometrial and cervical cancer, prolapse and heavy periods.

name: Pituitary gland
location: In the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.
description: A small gland with an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis).
function: Secretes hormones that regulate many other endocrine glands, growth, lactation and water balance.
clinicalRelevance: The optic chiasm lies just above the pituitary, so pituitary tumours can compress it and affect vision.

name: Thyroid gland
location: Anterior neck; two lobes joined by an isthmus that lies across the upper tracheal rings.
description: A butterfly-shaped gland made of follicles.
function: Secretes thyroid hormones (T3, T4), which regulate metabolic rate, and calcitonin.
clinicalRelevance: Hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism (Graves disease), goitre, nodules and thyroid cancer.

name: Parathyroid glands
location: Posterior surface of the thyroid gland; usually four.
description: Small glands embedded on the back of the thyroid lobes.
function: Secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium.
clinicalRelevance: Hyperparathyroidism causes high calcium, kidney stones and bone loss. Low calcium after thyroid surgery causes tingling and cramps.

name: Adrenal gland
location: On the superior pole of each kidney.
description: A gland with an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
function: The cortex secretes corticosteroids (such as cortisol and aldosterone); the medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine).
clinicalRelevance: Cushing syndrome, Addison disease, phaeochromocytoma and Conn syndrome.

name: Spleen
location: Left upper abdomen, behind the stomach and deep to the lower left ribs.
description: The largest lymphoid organ, containing red pulp and white pulp.
function: Filters blood, removes aged red blood cells and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures of the lower left ribs can rupture the spleen and cause serious internal bleeding.

sources.locator: Chapter 21: The Lymphatic and Immune System

name: Thymus
location: Superior and anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum.
description: A primary lymphoid organ that is large in childhood and gradually replaced by fat in adults.
function: Site of T-lymphocyte maturation.
clinicalRelevance: Myasthenia gravis, thymoma, and DiGeorge syndrome (a missing thymus with repeated infections).

sources.locator: Chapter 21: The Lymphatic and Immune System

name: Lymph nodes
location: Along lymphatic vessels, concentrated in regions such as the neck, axilla and groin.
description: Small encapsulated organs through which lymph is filtered as it returns towards the venous system. Most lymph ultimately drains via the thoracic duct into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
function: Filter lymph and allow lymphocytes to encounter antigens.
clinicalRelevance: Knowing which region drains to which node group helps explain where swollen nodes appear with infection or the spread of cancer.

sources.locator: Chapter 21: The Lymphatic and Immune System

name: Palatine tonsils
location: Lateral walls of the oropharynx.
description: Masses of lymphoid tissue forming part of a ring of tonsils around the pharynx.
function: Sample ingested and inhaled antigens and contribute to immune defence.
clinicalRelevance: Tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) and obstructed breathing in sleep in children.

sources.locator: Chapter 21: The Lymphatic and Immune System

name: Skin
location: Covers the external surface of the body.
description: The largest organ of the body, composed of the epidermis and dermis. The hypodermis lies beneath it.
function: Protection, temperature regulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis and prevention of water loss.
clinicalRelevance: Eczema, psoriasis, acne, skin infections, skin cancer (including melanoma) and burns.

name: Epidermis
description: The outer layer of skin: a keratinised stratified squamous epithelium without blood vessels.
function: Forms a protective, waterproof barrier and contains melanocytes that produce melanin.
clinicalRelevance: Sunburn, psoriasis, basal and squamous cell carcinoma and blistering diseases such as pemphigus.

name: Dermis
description: The connective tissue layer beneath the epidermis, with papillary and reticular layers. It contains blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands.
function: Provides strength and elasticity and supplies and supports the epidermis.
clinicalRelevance: Deep burns, scars and keloids, and connective tissue diseases.

name: Hypodermis
description: A layer of loose connective and adipose tissue beneath the dermis; not strictly part of the skin.
function: Anchors the skin to underlying structures, stores fat and provides insulation.
clinicalRelevance: Cellulitis, pressure sores and fat necrosis. It is the site for insulin and other injections under the skin.

name: Skin appendages
description: Hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands and nails, derived from the epidermis.
function: Sweat glands help cool the body; sebaceous glands secrete sebum that lubricates skin and hair; hair and nails protect underlying tissues.
clinicalRelevance: Hair loss (alopecia), acne (sebaceous glands), nail fungus and excessive sweating.

name: Eye
location: Within the bony orbit.
description: A globe with three layers: the outer fibrous layer (sclera and cornea), the vascular layer (choroid, ciliary body and iris) and the inner retina.
function: Focuses light onto the retina, whose photoreceptors convert it into nerve signals carried by the optic nerve (cranial nerve II).
clinicalRelevance: Cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, refractive errors and retinal detachment.

name: Ear
location: External ear on the side of the head; middle and inner ear within the temporal bone.
description: Divided into external, middle (tympanic cavity with ossicles) and inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus).
function: The cochlea detects sound; the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, utricle and saccule) detects head movement and position for balance. Both are served by the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII).
clinicalRelevance: Otitis media and externa, hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo (Meniere disease) and cholesteatoma.

name: Olfactory epithelium
location: Roof of the nasal cavity.
description: Specialised epithelium containing olfactory receptor neurons whose axons form the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I).
function: Detects odorant molecules.
clinicalRelevance: Loss of smell (anosmia) after viral infection, head injury or nasal polyps. It can be an early sign of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease.

name: Taste buds
location: Mainly on the papillae of the tongue.
description: Clusters of gustatory receptor cells and supporting cells.
function: Detect taste qualities; signals travel in cranial nerves VII, IX and X.
clinicalRelevance: Loss or change of taste from infection, zinc deficiency, medicines or chemotherapy.

name: Frontal lobe
location: Front of each cerebral hemisphere, ahead of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus.
description: The largest lobe of the cerebrum. Its precentral gyrus holds the primary motor cortex; the prefrontal region lies in front of it.
function: Planning, decision making, personality, attention and voluntary movement. In the dominant hemisphere Broca's area helps produce speech.
clinicalRelevance: Damage can change personality, judgement and motivation, and cause weakness on the opposite side of the body.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Parietal lobe
location: Upper back part of each hemisphere, between the central sulcus and the occipital lobe.
description: Contains the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) and association areas for space and body position.
function: Processes touch, pain, temperature and position sense, and builds awareness of space and of the body.
clinicalRelevance: Damage can cause neglect of one side of space, or trouble reading and calculating when the dominant side is affected.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Temporal lobe
location: Side of each hemisphere, below the lateral sulcus.
description: Contains the primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area on the dominant side, and the hippocampus on its inner surface.
function: Hearing, understanding speech, recognising objects and faces, and memory.
clinicalRelevance: A common origin of epileptic seizures. Damage to the dominant side can make speech hard to understand.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Occipital lobe
location: Back of each hemisphere, above the cerebellum.
description: Contains the primary visual cortex (area V1) along the calcarine sulcus.
function: Receives and first processes visual information.
clinicalRelevance: Damage causes loss of vision in part of the opposite visual field.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Insula
location: Folded cortex hidden deep inside the lateral sulcus.
description: A buried region of cortex covered by parts of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes.
function: Linked to taste, sensing the state of the body (interoception), pain and emotion.
clinicalRelevance: Stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory can damage it, causing loss of taste, altered pain perception and difficulty speaking. It can be the focus of seizures.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Hippocampus
location: Curved structure on the inner surface of the temporal lobe, beside the lateral ventricle.
description: A curved fold of cortex that belongs to the limbic system.
function: Helps form new long-term memories and supports spatial navigation.
clinicalRelevance: Among the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease. Loss on both sides causes severe difficulty forming new memories.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Deep cerebral structures
location: Deep inside each cerebral hemisphere, beneath the cortex.
description: In the Brain and skull model this groups the cerebral white matter (the fibre bundles that link cortical areas) with other deep structures. The exact contents follow the grouping of the source model.
function: Carries signals between cortical areas and between the cortex and the rest of the nervous system.
clinicalRelevance: Basal ganglia damage causes Parkinson disease and Huntington disease. Deep (lacunar) strokes from high blood pressure affect the thalamus and internal capsule.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Hypothalamus
location: Below the thalamus, forming the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle.
description: A small region at the base of the forebrain, connected to the pituitary gland by the infundibulum.
function: Regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep cycles and hormone release through the pituitary gland.
clinicalRelevance: Disorders cause diabetes insipidus and disturbed temperature, sleep, appetite and hormone control. Tumours such as craniopharyngioma press on it.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Midbrain
location: Uppermost part of the brainstem, between the pons and the diencephalon.
description: Contains the cerebral peduncles, the tectum (colliculi) and the substantia nigra.
function: Controls eye movements and visual and auditory reflexes, and contains dopamine-producing neurons.
clinicalRelevance: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Pons
location: Middle part of the brainstem, in front of the cerebellum.
description: A bulging band of fibres that bridges the midbrain and the medulla oblongata.
function: Relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum, contains nuclei of several cranial nerves and helps regulate breathing and sleep.
clinicalRelevance: Pontine stroke can cause locked-in syndrome. Central pontine myelinolysis follows too rapid correction of low blood sodium. Basilar artery blockage affects it.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Medulla oblongata
location: Lowest part of the brainstem, continuing into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
description: Contains the pyramids, the olives and nuclei of the lower cranial nerves.
function: Controls heart rate, breathing and reflexes such as swallowing and coughing. Most motor fibres cross to the opposite side here.
clinicalRelevance: Damage can be life threatening because it houses vital centres.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Lateral ventricles
location: One C-shaped cavity inside each cerebral hemisphere.
description: The largest cavities of the ventricular system, each with a body, anterior, posterior and inferior horn.
function: Make and hold cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the choroid plexus. Each drains to the third ventricle through an interventricular foramen.
clinicalRelevance: Blocked drainage lets CSF build up and causes hydrocephalus.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Third ventricle
location: Narrow midline slit between the two halves of the thalamus.
description: A slit-like cavity whose walls include the thalamus and hypothalamus.
function: Receives CSF from both lateral ventricles and passes it on through the cerebral aqueduct.
clinicalRelevance: A colloid cyst can block the interventricular foramina and cause hydrocephalus. Tumours of the pineal region press on the nearby aqueduct.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Cerebral aqueduct
location: Narrow canal running through the midbrain.
description: A thin channel that joins the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.
function: Carries CSF from the third to the fourth ventricle.
clinicalRelevance: Because it is so narrow it is a common place for a blockage (aqueductal stenosis) leading to hydrocephalus.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Fourth ventricle
location: Diamond-shaped cavity behind the pons and medulla, in front of the cerebellum.
description: The last cavity of the ventricular system, continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord.
function: CSF leaves the ventricles here, through the median and lateral apertures, and enters the space around the brain and spinal cord.
clinicalRelevance: Blocked outflow (Dandy-Walker malformation, medulloblastoma, ependymoma) causes hydrocephalus. Bleeding from the cerebellum can burst into it.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Cerebral arterial circle
location: Ring of arteries on the underside of the brain, around the pituitary stalk and optic chiasm.
description: Joins the two internal carotid arteries and the basilar artery through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries.
function: Links the carotid and vertebrobasilar blood supplies, giving back-up routes if one vessel narrows.
clinicalRelevance: A common site for berry aneurysms.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Internal carotid artery
location: Rises in the neck from the common carotid artery, enters the skull through the carotid canal, passes through the cavernous sinus and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
description: One of the two main arteries of the brain. It has no branches in the neck. Here the part inside the skull comes from the BodyParts3D scan data.
function: Carries oxygenated blood to the front and much of the cerebral hemispheres, and to the eye through the ophthalmic artery.
clinicalRelevance: Narrowing (atherosclerosis) of the internal carotid artery is a common cause of ischaemic stroke and of brief loss of vision in one eye. A carotid endarterectomy removes the plaque.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Vertebral artery
location: Arises from the subclavian artery, rises through the transverse foramina of the upper cervical vertebrae and enters the skull through the foramen magnum.
description: Paired arteries of the back of the brain. They join in front of the medulla to form the basilar artery. Only the part near the skull is shown in this model.
function: Supplies the brainstem, cerebellum and upper spinal cord, and with the basilar artery the occipital lobes.
clinicalRelevance: A tear (dissection) of the vertebral artery after neck injury can cause a stroke in the back of the brain.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Basilar artery
location: Runs up the front of the pons, from the union of the two vertebral arteries to its division into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
description: A single midline artery of the posterior circulation.
function: Supplies the pons, midbrain and cerebellum through its branches, and feeds both posterior cerebral arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Blockage of the basilar artery can cause "locked-in" syndrome and is often fatal.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Anterior cerebral artery
location: Runs forward from the internal carotid artery, then arches back over the corpus callosum as the pericallosal artery. The two sides are joined by the anterior communicating artery.
description: The smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery. The first part is from scan data; the arch over the corpus callosum and the cortical branches are schematic.
function: Supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage mainly causes weakness and numbness of the opposite leg.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Middle cerebral artery
location: Runs sideways from the internal carotid artery into the lateral sulcus, then fans out over the side of the hemisphere.
description: The larger terminal branch of the internal carotid artery. The scan data holds only the right side; the left side here is a mirror image. Cortical branches are schematic.
function: Supplies most of the outer surface of the hemisphere (face and arm areas of the motor and sensory cortex, auditory and language areas) and, through small lenticulostriate branches, deep structures such as the internal capsule.
clinicalRelevance: The most common artery involved in ischaemic stroke: weakness and numbness of the opposite face and arm, and language problems if the dominant side is affected.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Posterior cerebral artery
location: Curves around the midbrain from the end of the basilar artery to the occipital lobe and the underside of the temporal lobe.
description: Terminal branch of the basilar artery in most people. The part around the midbrain is drawn schematically.
function: Supplies the occipital lobe (visual cortex), the lower temporal lobe, the thalamus and the midbrain.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage causes loss of vision in the opposite half of the visual field.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superior cerebellar artery
location: Arises from the basilar artery just below its end and runs round the upper pons to the top of the cerebellum.
description: A branch of the basilar artery.
function: Supplies the upper surface of the cerebellum, part of the pons and the midbrain.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage can cause unsteadiness (ataxia) and vertigo.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
location: Arises from the lower basilar artery and runs to the front underside of the cerebellum.
description: A branch of the basilar artery that often gives off the labyrinthine artery to the inner ear.
function: Supplies the front underside of the cerebellum and the lower pons.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage can cause vertigo, hearing loss and facial weakness.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
location: Arises from the vertebral artery, loops around the medulla and supplies the underside of the cerebellum.
description: The largest branch of the vertebral artery.
function: Supplies the lateral medulla and the lower back part of the cerebellum.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: dizziness, difficulty swallowing and loss of pain and temperature sense.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Pontine arteries
location: Small branches that leave the basilar artery and enter the pons.
description: Several short branches of the basilar artery.
function: Supply the pons.
clinicalRelevance: Small-vessel blockage causes small deep strokes (lacunes) in the pons.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Ophthalmic artery
location: Arises from the internal carotid artery as it leaves the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the optic canal.
description: The first large branch of the internal carotid artery after the cavernous sinus.
function: Supplies the eye, the orbit and part of the forehead and nose. Its branch, the central retinal artery, supplies the retina.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage of the central retinal artery causes sudden painless loss of vision in one eye.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Anterior choroidal artery
location: Arises from the internal carotid artery and runs back to the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.
description: A thin branch of the internal carotid artery.
function: Supplies the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle, the optic tract, part of the internal capsule and the hippocampus.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage can cause weakness and numbness of the opposite side and a visual field defect.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Posterior choroidal arteries
location: Arise from the posterior cerebral artery and run forward to the roof of the third ventricle.
description: Small branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
function: Supply the choroid plexus of the third and lateral ventricles and the thalamus.
clinicalRelevance: Blockage contributes to infarcts in the thalamus and next to the ventricles. They feed the choroid plexus that makes CSF.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Thalamic perforating arteries
location: Arise from the posterior cerebral artery near its origin and enter the brain through the posterior perforated substance.
description: Small penetrating branches of the posterior circulation.
function: Supply the thalamus and the upper midbrain.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage can cause loss of sensation, drowsiness or memory problems.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Anterior spinal artery
location: Forms from branches of both vertebral arteries and runs down the front of the medulla and spinal cord.
description: A single artery on the midline of the front of the spinal cord. Only its upper end is shown.
function: Supplies the front two thirds of the spinal cord and part of the medulla.
clinicalRelevance: A blockage causes loss of movement and of pain and temperature sense below the level, with touch and position sense kept.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superior sagittal sinus
location: Runs in the midline along the upper edge of the falx cerebri, from the front of the skull to the confluence of sinuses at the back.
description: The largest dural venous sinus. Dural sinuses are channels between layers of dura mater with no muscle in their walls. Position and size are schematic.
function: Drains the superior cerebral veins and receives CSF through arachnoid granulations. It usually empties into the right transverse sinus.
clinicalRelevance: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis causes headache, raised pressure in the skull and seizures.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Inferior sagittal sinus
location: Runs along the lower free edge of the falx cerebri above the corpus callosum.
description: A small sinus that joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. Schematic.
function: Drains the medial surfaces of the hemispheres and part of the falx.
clinicalRelevance: It is rarely blocked on its own. Thrombosis of the venous sinuses in general causes headache, seizures and venous infarcts.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Straight sinus
location: Runs back along the line where the falx cerebri meets the tentorium cerebelli, to the confluence of sinuses.
description: Formed by the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein. Schematic.
function: Carries blood from the deep parts of the brain to the transverse sinus, usually on the left.
clinicalRelevance: Thrombosis causes deep venous infarction of the thalamus and basal ganglia, with headache and drowsiness or coma.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Great cerebral vein
location: Short vein below the back end of the corpus callosum, formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins.
description: A short, wide vein that drains the deep brain into the straight sinus. Schematic.
function: Drains deep structures such as the thalamus, basal ganglia and choroid plexus.
clinicalRelevance: Malformations of the vein of Galen can cause heart failure in newborns.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Internal cerebral veins
location: Run back in the roof of the third ventricle from the interventricular foramina.
description: A pair of deep veins that unite to form the great cerebral vein. Schematic.
function: Drain the thalamus, striatum and choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles.
clinicalRelevance: Thrombosis causes infarction of both thalami with drowsiness and coma.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Transverse sinus
location: Runs sideways along the back edge of the tentorium cerebelli from the confluence of sinuses to the petrous part of the temporal bone.
description: Paired sinuses, usually larger on the right. Schematic position.
function: Carry blood from the superior sagittal and straight sinuses to the sigmoid sinuses.
clinicalRelevance: Thrombosis here can raise pressure inside the skull.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Sigmoid sinus
location: S-shaped continuation of the transverse sinus, grooving the mastoid part of the temporal bone to the jugular foramen.
description: Continues as the internal jugular vein. Schematic position.
function: Carries blood out of the skull.
clinicalRelevance: Infection of the middle ear or mastoid can spread to the sigmoid sinus and cause thrombosis.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Internal jugular vein
location: Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and runs down the neck in the carotid sheath beside the carotid artery.
description: The main vein of the head and neck. Only its upper part is shown here.
function: Carries blood from the brain, face and neck towards the heart. It joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
clinicalRelevance: The jugular venous pressure is read from it to estimate pressure in the right side of the heart. It is a common site for central venous catheters.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Cavernous sinus
location: One on each side of the sella turcica and pituitary gland.
description: A venous space that contains the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. Schematic.
function: Drains the eye, the front of the brain and part of the face into the petrosal sinuses.
clinicalRelevance: Infection of the face can spread to it and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Petrosal sinuses
location: Run along the upper and lower borders of the petrous part of the temporal bone.
description: Small sinuses that link the cavernous sinus to the transverse sinus and internal jugular vein. This model shows one schematic channel per side.
function: Carry blood from the cavernous sinus out of the skull.
clinicalRelevance: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is used to find the source of Cushing disease. Ear infection (mastoiditis) can spread to them.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superficial cerebral veins
location: Run on the surface of the hemispheres in the subarachnoid space.
description: Thin veins that collect blood from the cortex and empty into the nearest dural sinus. The pattern shown is schematic.
function: Drain the cortex and underlying white matter: upward veins reach the superior sagittal sinus, lower and back veins reach the transverse sinus, and front and lower veins reach the cavernous sinus.
clinicalRelevance: Bridging veins cross the subdural space and can tear in a head injury, causing a subdural haematoma.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Cerebral capillary bed
location: Throughout the brain tissue, densest in grey matter.
description: A fine network of microscopic vessels between the smallest arteries (arterioles) and the smallest veins (venules). The loops here are drawn schematically and much larger than real capillaries, which are only about 7 micrometres wide.
function: Exchanges oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide and wastes with brain tissue. Tight junctions between endothelial cells, supported by astrocytes, form the blood-brain barrier.
clinicalRelevance: The blood-brain barrier keeps many drugs out of the brain. It can break down in stroke, infection and tumours.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Subarachnoid space
location: Between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater that covers the brain and spinal cord.
description: The space that holds cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) around the brain and spinal cord. It is crossed by fine strands (trabeculae) and carries the cerebral arteries and veins. Drawn as a thin translucent layer about 2.5 mm thick; in life its width varies.
function: The fluid floats the brain, cushions it against knocks and carries nutrients and wastes. Fluid returns to the blood through arachnoid granulations.
clinicalRelevance: A ruptured aneurysm bleeds into this space (subarachnoid haemorrhage). A lumbar puncture takes CSF from the lower end of the space. Meningitis is infection of it.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Subarachnoid cisterns
location: Where the arachnoid mater bridges larger gaps between brain surfaces.
description: Wider pools of CSF. This model shows the cerebellomedullary cistern (cisterna magna), the prepontine cistern, the quadrigeminal cistern and the chiasmatic cistern.
function: Hold CSF and surround large arteries and cranial nerves at the base of the brain. CSF leaves the fourth ventricle into the cisterna magna.
clinicalRelevance: Blood in the basal cisterns on a CT scan points to a subarachnoid haemorrhage.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Choroid plexus
location: In the lateral ventricles (body and horns), the roof of the third ventricle and the roof of the fourth ventricle.
description: Folds of blood vessels covered by a layer of ependymal cells. The model shows a schematic ribbon in each lateral ventricle only.
function: Makes most of the CSF: about 500 mL a day, so the total volume of about 150 mL is renewed several times daily.
clinicalRelevance: A choroid plexus papilloma can make too much CSF and cause hydrocephalus.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Arachnoid granulations
location: Along the superior sagittal sinus, mainly on each side of the midline.
description: Small tufts of arachnoid mater that push through the dura into the venous sinuses. Schematic positions.
function: Act as one-way valves that let CSF flow into the venous blood of the sinus.
clinicalRelevance: If absorption fails the pressure rises (communicating hydrocephalus). They can wear small pits in the skull.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Anterior cranial fossa
location: Front part of the floor of the skull.
description: The shallow front floor of the cranial cavity: orbital parts of the frontal bone, the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and the lesser wings of the sphenoid. The region is cut from the scan bones by simple planes.
function: Holds the frontal lobes and the olfactory bulbs and forms the roof of the eye sockets and nose.
clinicalRelevance: A fracture of the cribriform plate can tear the meninges, leak CSF from the nose and cause loss of smell.

name: Middle cranial fossa
location: Middle part of the floor of the skull, behind the lesser wings of the sphenoid.
description: A butterfly-shaped hollow formed by the body and greater wings of the sphenoid and the squamous and front petrous parts of the temporal bone. The region is cut from the scan bones by simple planes.
function: Holds the temporal lobes and, in the sella turcica, the pituitary gland. Openings carry cranial nerves II to VI and the middle meningeal artery.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures here can tear the middle meningeal artery or injure cranial nerves.

name: Posterior cranial fossa
location: Back and lowest part of the floor of the skull, behind the petrous ridges.
description: The deepest and largest fossa, formed mainly by the occipital bone and the back of the petrous temporal bones. The region is cut from the scan bones by simple planes.
function: Holds the cerebellum, pons and medulla. The foramen magnum, jugular foramen and internal acoustic meatus open into it.
clinicalRelevance: Swelling here can block the fourth ventricle (hydrocephalus) or push the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum and press on the medulla.

name: Calvaria (skull cap)
location: The upper dome of the skull above the cranial base.
description: The vault formed by the frontal bone, the two parietal bones and the upper occipital and temporal bones, joined by the coronal, sagittal and lambdoid sutures.
function: Protects the upper brain.
clinicalRelevance: A skull fracture at the thin side (pterion) can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an extradural haematoma.

name: Corticospinal tract
location: From the motor cortex through the corona radiata, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, pons and the pyramid of the medulla, then down the lateral column of the spinal cord.
description: The main pathway for voluntary movement. About 85-90% of its fibres cross to the other side in the pyramidal decussation at the bottom of the medulla, so each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. Paths are drawn schematically as thin tubes.
function: Carries movement commands from the cortex to the motor neurons of the spinal cord, which in turn drive the muscles through peripheral nerves.
clinicalRelevance: A stroke above the decussation causes weakness on the opposite side of the body. Damage to this tract gives an upper motor neuron picture: weakness, raised tone and brisk reflexes.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Dorsal column - medial lemniscus pathway
latinName: Via columnae posteriores et lemnisci medialis
location: Up the back (dorsal) columns of the spinal cord on the same side, to the gracile and cuneate nuclei in the medulla, where it crosses, then up the medial lemniscus to the thalamus and the sensory cortex.
description: The pathway for fine touch, vibration and joint position sense. Paths are drawn schematically as thin tubes.
function: Brings precise touch and body position information from the limbs to the opposite side of the brain.
clinicalRelevance: Damage to the dorsal columns (for example in vitamin B12 deficiency or syphilis) causes loss of position sense and an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Spinothalamic tract
location: Fibres enter the spinal cord, cross to the opposite side within a few segments, and run up the front and side of the cord and the brainstem to the thalamus and the sensory cortex.
description: The pathway for pain, temperature and crude touch. Paths are drawn schematically as thin tubes.
function: Carries pain and temperature signals from the body to the opposite side of the brain.
clinicalRelevance: A lesion on one side of the cord causes loss of position sense on that side and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side (Brown-Sequard syndrome).

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Dura mater
location: The outermost meningeal layer, lining the inside of the skull and the vertebral canal.
description: A thick, tough layer of dense connective tissue. In the skull it fuses with the periosteum and forms folds (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli) and the dural venous sinuses. Around the cord it is separated from the vertebrae by the epidural space. Drawn here as a smooth shell (tan).
function: Protects the brain and holds it in place. Its sinuses drain blood from the brain.
