clinicalRelevance: A tear of a middle meningeal artery (epidural haematoma) or of bridging veins under the dura (subdural haematoma) can compress the brain.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Arachnoid mater
location: The middle meningeal layer, just under the dura, spanning the grooves of the brain.
description: A thin, web-like membrane. Below it lies the subarachnoid space with the CSF; it is crossed by fine strands and carries the cerebral arteries and veins. Drawn here as a smooth, pale shell.
function: Forms the outer wall of the subarachnoid space and, through the arachnoid granulations, lets CSF pass into the venous sinuses.
clinicalRelevance: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space (for example from a ruptured aneurysm) causes a sudden severe headache. Infection here is meningitis.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Pia mater
location: The innermost meningeal layer, closely covering the surface of the brain and spinal cord and following every groove.
description: A very thin, delicate membrane rich in small blood vessels. Drawn here as a pink shell right on the brain surface.
function: Supports the vessels that enter the brain and separates the brain tissue from the CSF.
clinicalRelevance: Together with the arachnoid it is the site of meningitis.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Right upper lobe
location: Above the horizontal fissure, behind the first to fourth ribs at the front.
description: The highest of the three lobes of the right lung, with apical, posterior and anterior bronchopulmonary segments.
function: Takes part in gas exchange, mainly in the upper chest.
clinicalRelevance: Pneumonia, tuberculosis (which often starts at the apex), and lung cancers (Pancoast tumour at the apex).

name: Right middle lobe
location: Between the horizontal and oblique fissures, at the front of the right chest.
description: The smallest lobe of the right lung, with lateral and medial segments. It lies against the right side of the heart.
function: Takes part in gas exchange.
clinicalRelevance: Middle lobe syndrome: its narrow bronchus is easily squeezed by lymph nodes, causing collapse and repeated infection.

name: Right lower lobe
location: Below the oblique fissure, resting on the diaphragm at the back of the right chest.
description: The largest lobe of the right lung, with a superior and four basal segments.
function: Takes part in gas exchange, mainly when breathing deeply at the base.
clinicalRelevance: Aspiration pneumonia (food or fluid breathed in usually passes to the right lower lobe), abscess, and bronchiectasis.

name: Left upper lobe
location: Above the oblique fissure, with the cardiac notch and the lingula at its lower front.
description: Equal to the right upper and middle lobes together. The lingula is the tongue-shaped part that matches the right middle lobe.
function: Takes part in gas exchange.
clinicalRelevance: Pneumonia, lung cancer, and tuberculosis. The lingula can collapse or become infected.

name: Left lower lobe
location: Below the oblique fissure, resting on the left side of the diaphragm.
description: The large lower lobe of the left lung with a superior and four basal segments.
function: Takes part in gas exchange.
clinicalRelevance: Pneumonia, lung abscess, and collapse (atelectasis), common after surgery.

name: Bronchioles
location: Inside the lungs, beyond the segmental bronchi.
description: The small airways with no cartilage in their walls, about 1 mm across or less, ending in the respiratory bronchioles that open into the alveoli. The branching here is schematic.
function: Their smooth muscle widens and narrows the airways and so controls the flow of air.
clinicalRelevance: Asthma (the muscle tightens and the lining swells), bronchiolitis in infants, and COPD.

name: Bronchial tree
location: Inside both lungs, from the carina to the terminal bronchioles.
description: The branching airways: main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi and about 23 generations of divisions down to the alveolar sacs. The scan shows the larger airways, and the finer branches and alveoli are drawn schematically.
function: Carries air to and from the alveoli, warms, humidifies and filters it. Cilia and mucus clear dust and microbes.
clinicalRelevance: Asthma, chronic bronchitis, COPD, bronchiectasis, lung cancer and inhaled foreign bodies.

name: Respiratory bronchiole
location: The last airways of the bronchial tree, at the edge of the lung tissue.
description: A tiny airway, about 0.5 mm wide, whose wall has a few alveoli budding from it, so some gas exchange already takes place here.
function: Leads air from the terminal bronchioles to the alveolar ducts.
clinicalRelevance: Damaged in emphysema and in smoking-related small airway disease.

name: Alveolar duct
location: Between the respiratory bronchiole and the alveolar sacs.
description: A short passage whose walls are almost entirely made of the openings of alveoli.
function: Brings air to the clusters of alveoli (alveolar sacs).
clinicalRelevance: Fibrosis and emphysema destroy or scar the walls of the alveolar ducts and sacs.

name: Pulmonary capillaries
location: In the alveolar walls, wrapped around every alveolus.
description: A dense net of capillaries about 7 micrometres wide. A red blood cell passes through in under a second. The wall is shared with the alveolus, so the blood-air barrier is only about 0.5 micrometres thick.
function: Blood picks up oxygen from the alveolar air and gives up carbon dioxide. The red blood cells here turn from dark purple to bright red.
clinicalRelevance: Pulmonary oedema (fluid leaks into the alveoli), pulmonary embolism (a clot blocks the flow) and pulmonary fibrosis (a thick wall slows gas exchange).

name: Pulmonary arteriole
location: Beside the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
description: A small branch of the pulmonary artery. It carries blood low in oxygen (shown blue) to the capillaries.
function: Delivers deoxygenated blood from the right heart to the alveolar capillaries.
clinicalRelevance: Narrows in response to low oxygen (to match blood flow to ventilation); pulmonary hypertension develops when it stays narrowed.

name: Pulmonary venule
location: Between the alveoli, joining to form the pulmonary veins.
description: A small vessel that collects blood rich in oxygen (shown red) from the capillaries.
function: Returns oxygenated blood towards the pulmonary veins and the left atrium.
clinicalRelevance: Congestion of these veins from left heart failure causes breathlessness and fluid in the lungs.

name: Type II pneumocyte
location: Scattered in the corners of the alveolar wall.
description: A rounded cell that makes surfactant and can divide to repair the wall. It makes up about 5% of the alveolar surface, but about 60% of the cells.
function: Makes surfactant, a film of fat and protein that lowers surface tension so that the alveoli do not collapse when you breathe out.
clinicalRelevance: Premature babies lack surfactant and develop respiratory distress syndrome. Damage to these cells contributes to ARDS and to pulmonary fibrosis.

name: Alveolar macrophage
location: Free on the inner surface of the alveoli.
description: A scavenger white cell that lives in the alveolar air space.
function: Engulfs dust, bacteria and other particles that get past the airway defences.
clinicalRelevance: Overloaded macrophages in smokers and in silicosis release enzymes and signals that damage the lungs; in tuberculosis the bacteria live inside macrophages.

name: Inferior phrenic artery
location: Arises from the abdominal aorta (or the coeliac trunk) at the aortic opening and runs up on the underside of the diaphragm.
description: The main artery of the diaphragm. Each side divides into an anterior and a posterior branch that spread over the abdominal surface of the muscle. The right artery passes behind the inferior vena cava.
function: Supplies the diaphragm with oxygen-rich blood. Branches also reach the adrenal gland. The matching veins drain into the inferior vena cava on the right and the left adrenal or renal vein on the left.
clinicalRelevance: Rich links (anastomoses) with the other phrenic arteries protect the diaphragm if one vessel is blocked. A liver cancer can grow extra feeding vessels from this artery, which matters when its blood supply is blocked by radiology treatment. Cuts or tears of the diaphragm from stab wounds or accidents can bleed from these branches.

name: Superior phrenic artery
location: Arises from the lower thoracic aorta and runs on the upper (chest) surface of the back of the diaphragm.
description: A small artery, often several twigs, to the back of the diaphragm. It joins the inferior phrenic, musculophrenic and pericardiophrenic arteries.
function: Supplies the back and top of the diaphragm.
clinicalRelevance: Because of the many links with the other phrenic arteries, blocking this vessel rarely harms the diaphragm. Its twigs can bleed in chest injuries with tears of the diaphragm.

name: Musculophrenic artery
location: A branch of the internal thoracic artery. It runs along the lower rib margin (costal margin) on the chest side of the diaphragm.
description: The terminal branch of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery. It follows the edge of the diaphragm where it joins the lower ribs and gives branches to the lower intercostal spaces.
function: Supplies the front and sides of the diaphragm, the lower chest wall and the upper abdominal wall.
clinicalRelevance: The internal thoracic artery is often used as a graft in heart bypass surgery, but the musculophrenic branch is usually left in place. Wounds along the lower rib margin can injure it.

name: Pericardiophrenic artery
location: A branch of the internal thoracic artery. It runs with the phrenic nerve between the pericardium and the pleura.
description: A long, thin artery that travels beside the phrenic nerve down to the diaphragm.
function: Supplies the pericardium, the pleura beside it and the top of the diaphragm.
clinicalRelevance: During heart or lung surgery the artery and the phrenic nerve run together and can be injured together. This may cause a raised, weak half of the diaphragm.

name: Lower intercostal and subcostal nerves
latinName: Nervi intercostales inferiores et nervus subcostalis
location: Along the rim of the diaphragm, where it attaches to the lower six ribs and their cartilages.
description: The lower six intercostal nerves and the subcostal nerve give sensory branches to the outer rim of the diaphragm.
function: Carry pain and touch sensation from the edge of the diaphragm. They do not move the muscle: all of its movement (motor supply) comes from the phrenic nerves.
clinicalRelevance: Irritation of the rim of the diaphragm (for example in pleurisy or pneumonia of the lower lung) can cause pain felt in the lower chest or upper abdominal wall. Irritation of the centre is felt as shoulder-tip pain because it travels in the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).

name: Supraspinatus
location: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula, under the acromion.
description: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula, under the acromion.
function: Starts abduction of the arm (first 15 degrees) and holds the humeral head in the shoulder socket.
origin: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula.
insertion: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
actions: Starts abduction of the arm (first 15 degrees) and holds the humeral head in the shoulder socket.
clinicalRelevance: The most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle. A painful arc of movement between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction suggests a tendon problem under the acromion.

name: Infraspinatus
location: Infraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula.
description: Infraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula.
function: Rotates the arm outward (lateral rotation) and stabilises the shoulder joint.
origin: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula.
insertion: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
actions: Rotates the arm outward (lateral rotation) and stabilises the shoulder joint.
clinicalRelevance: Part of the rotator cuff. Weakness of outward rotation suggests a cuff tear or injury of the suprascapular nerve.

name: Teres minor
location: Back of the shoulder, below infraspinatus.
description: Back of the shoulder, below infraspinatus.
function: Rotates the arm outward and holds the humeral head in the socket.
origin: Upper two-thirds of the lateral border of the scapula.
insertion: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
actions: Rotates the arm outward and holds the humeral head in the socket.
clinicalRelevance: Part of the rotator cuff. Axillary nerve damage (for example after a shoulder dislocation) weakens it together with deltoid.

name: Teres major
location: Back of the shoulder, below teres minor.
description: Back of the shoulder, below teres minor.
function: Rotates the arm inward, adducts it and extends it from a flexed position.
origin: Inferior angle and lower lateral border of the scapula.
insertion: Medial lip of the bicipital groove of the humerus.
actions: Rotates the arm inward, adducts it and extends it from a flexed position.
clinicalRelevance: Forms the lower border of the quadrangular space. It is not part of the rotator cuff.

name: Subscapularis
location: Front of the scapula, forming the back wall of the armpit.
description: Front of the scapula, forming the back wall of the armpit.
function: Rotates the arm inward and stabilises the front of the shoulder joint.
origin: Subscapular fossa of the scapula.
insertion: Lesser tubercle of the humerus.
innervation: Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, C6, C7).
actions: Rotates the arm inward and stabilises the front of the shoulder joint.
clinicalRelevance: The strongest rotator cuff muscle. A positive "lift-off" test suggests a tear.

name: Coracobrachialis
location: Upper inner arm, in the front compartment.
description: Upper inner arm, in the front compartment.
function: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
origin: Tip of the coracoid process of the scapula.
insertion: Middle of the medial surface of the humerus.
actions: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
clinicalRelevance: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it, which is a landmark when finding the nerve.

name: Brachialis
location: Deep to biceps brachii in the front of the arm.
description: Deep to biceps brachii in the front of the arm.
function: The main flexor of the elbow, in every position of the forearm.
origin: Distal half of the front of the humerus.
insertion: Ulnar tuberosity and coronoid process of the ulna.
innervation: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6) and a small branch of the radial nerve.
actions: The main flexor of the elbow, in every position of the forearm.
clinicalRelevance: A supracondylar fracture of the humerus can injure the brachial artery and the nerves close to this muscle.

name: Anconeus
location: Small triangular muscle behind the elbow.
description: Small triangular muscle behind the elbow.
function: Helps triceps extend the elbow and steadies the elbow joint.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (back).
insertion: Lateral side of the olecranon and the upper back of the ulna.
actions: Helps triceps extend the elbow and steadies the elbow joint.
bloodSupply: Posterior interosseous and middle collateral arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Can be involved in lateral elbow pain together with the extensor tendons.

name: Latissimus dorsi
location: Large flat muscle of the back and lower chest wall.
description: Large flat muscle of the back and lower chest wall.
function: Extends, adducts and rotates the arm inward. It is used when climbing or pulling the body up.
origin: Spinous processes of T7 to L5 and the sacrum (thoracolumbar fascia), the back of the iliac crest, lower three or four ribs.
insertion: Floor of the bicipital groove of the humerus.
actions: Extends, adducts and rotates the arm inward. It is used when climbing or pulling the body up.
bloodSupply: Thoracodorsal artery and posterior intercostal arteries.
clinicalRelevance: The muscle is used as a flap in breast reconstruction. Damage to the thoracodorsal nerve in axillary surgery weakens pulling.

name: Rhomboid major
location: Between the spine and the shoulder blade.
description: Between the spine and the shoulder blade.
function: Pulls the scapula towards the spine and holds it against the chest wall.
origin: Spinous processes of T2 to T5.
insertion: Medial border of the scapula below the spine.
actions: Pulls the scapula towards the spine and holds it against the chest wall.
clinicalRelevance: Injury of the dorsal scapular nerve causes a winged shoulder blade that tilts slightly.

name: Rhomboid minor
location: Between the spine and the shoulder blade, above rhomboid major.
description: Between the spine and the shoulder blade, above rhomboid major.
function: Pulls the scapula towards the spine and holds it against the chest wall.
origin: Lower ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 and T1.
insertion: Medial border of the scapula at the root of the spine.
actions: Pulls the scapula towards the spine and holds it against the chest wall.
clinicalRelevance: Strain between the shoulder blades is common with poor posture.

name: Levator scapulae
location: Side and back of the neck, running to the shoulder blade.
description: Side and back of the neck, running to the shoulder blade.
function: Lifts the scapula (shrugging) and tilts its lower angle towards the spine.
origin: Transverse processes of C1 to C4.
insertion: Medial border of the scapula from the top to the root of the spine.
innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves C3, C4.
actions: Lifts the scapula (shrugging) and tilts its lower angle towards the spine.
bloodSupply: Dorsal scapular and transverse cervical arteries.
clinicalRelevance: A frequent source of neck and shoulder tension.

name: Serratus anterior
location: Side of the chest wall under the armpit.
description: Side of the chest wall under the armpit.
function: Pulls the scapula forward around the chest wall and holds it flat. It also turns the scapula to raise the arm above shoulder height.
origin: Outer surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs.
insertion: Front of the medial border of the scapula.
actions: Pulls the scapula forward around the chest wall and holds it flat. It also turns the scapula to raise the arm above shoulder height.
clinicalRelevance: Long thoracic nerve injury (for example in breast or axillary surgery) causes a winged scapula that sticks out when pushing against a wall.

name: Pectoralis minor
location: Deep to pectoralis major, in the upper front chest.
description: Deep to pectoralis major, in the upper front chest.
function: Pulls the scapula forward and down, and lifts the ribs when the scapula is fixed.
origin: Outer surfaces of ribs 3 to 5 near their cartilages.
insertion: Medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process of the scapula.
innervation: Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1) and lateral pectoral nerve.
actions: Pulls the scapula forward and down, and lifts the ribs when the scapula is fixed.
clinicalRelevance: The axillary artery and brachial plexus pass behind it. Tightness can compress them (pectoralis minor syndrome).

name: Trapezius
location: Back of the neck and upper back, from the skull to T12.
description: Back of the neck and upper back, from the skull to T12.
function: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula. The upper fibres shrug the shoulder; the lower fibres pull it down.
origin: Superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T12.
insertion: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula.
innervation: Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) for movement; C3 and C4 for pain and position sense.
actions: Elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula. The upper fibres shrug the shoulder; the lower fibres pull it down.
bloodSupply: Transverse cervical artery and dorsal scapular artery.
clinicalRelevance: Damage to the accessory nerve (neck surgery or lymph node biopsy) causes a drooping shoulder and weakness of shrugging.

name: Pronator teres
location: Front of the forearm, running obliquely from the inner elbow.
description: Front of the forearm, running obliquely from the inner elbow.
function: Turns the forearm so the palm faces down (pronation) and helps flex the elbow.
origin: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: coronoid process of the ulna.
insertion: Middle of the lateral surface of the radius.
actions: Turns the forearm so the palm faces down (pronation) and helps flex the elbow.
clinicalRelevance: The median nerve passes between its two heads and can be trapped there (pronator syndrome).

name: Flexor carpi radialis
location: Front of the forearm, on the thumb side.
description: Front of the forearm, on the thumb side.
function: Flexes and abducts the wrist (radial deviation).
origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon).
insertion: Bases of the second and third metacarpal bones.
actions: Flexes and abducts the wrist (radial deviation).
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon is a landmark for the radial pulse and for the median nerve at the wrist.

name: Palmaris longus
location: Front of the forearm, a slender muscle with a long tendon.
description: Front of the forearm, a slender muscle with a long tendon.
function: Weakly flexes the wrist and tightens the palmar fascia.
origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus.
insertion: Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis.
actions: Weakly flexes the wrist and tightens the palmar fascia.
clinicalRelevance: Absent in about 15 per cent of people. Its tendon is often used as a graft in hand surgery.

name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
location: Front of the forearm on the little finger side.
description: Front of the forearm on the little finger side.
function: Flexes and adducts the wrist (ulnar deviation).
origin: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: olecranon and the upper back of the ulna.
insertion: Pisiform bone, then hook of the hamate and the fifth metacarpal by ligaments.
actions: Flexes and adducts the wrist (ulnar deviation).
clinicalRelevance: The ulnar nerve runs between its two heads in the cubital tunnel. Compression there causes numbness of the little finger.

name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
location: Middle layer of the front of the forearm.
description: Middle layer of the front of the forearm.
function: Flexes the middle joints of the fingers, then the knuckles and the wrist.
origin: Humeroulnar head: medial epicondyle, ulnar collateral ligament and coronoid process. Radial head: upper half of the anterior border of the radius.
insertion: Sides of the middle phalanges of the four fingers.
actions: Flexes the middle joints of the fingers, then the knuckles and the wrist.
clinicalRelevance: Tendon injuries in the palm ("no man's land") need careful repair. The median nerve runs deep to the muscle.

name: Flexor digitorum profundus
location: Deep layer of the front of the forearm.
description: Deep layer of the front of the forearm.
function: Flexes the tip joints of the fingers. It is the only muscle that bends the end joint.
origin: Upper three-quarters of the front and medial surfaces of the ulna and the interosseous membrane.
insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of the four fingers.
innervation: Medial half (ring and little fingers): ulnar nerve. Lateral half (index and middle fingers): anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Flexes the tip joints of the fingers. It is the only muscle that bends the end joint.
clinicalRelevance: A torn tendon from a sudden pull on a gripped finger ("jersey finger") prevents bending the fingertip.

name: Flexor pollicis longus
location: Deep front of the forearm on the thumb side.
description: Deep front of the forearm on the thumb side.
function: Flexes the tip joint of the thumb.
origin: Front of the radius and the adjacent interosseous membrane.
insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb.
innervation: Anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve, C8, T1).
actions: Flexes the tip joint of the thumb.
clinicalRelevance: Loss of thumb tip flexion with a pinch like an "OK sign" suggests an anterior interosseous nerve lesion.

name: Pronator quadratus
location: Front of the lower forearm, just above the wrist.
description: Front of the lower forearm, just above the wrist.
function: Pronates the forearm and holds the radius and ulna together at the wrist.
origin: Distal quarter of the front of the ulna.
insertion: Distal quarter of the front of the radius.
actions: Pronates the forearm and holds the radius and ulna together at the wrist.
clinicalRelevance: A fracture of the distal radius can displace or injure it.

name: Brachioradialis
location: Along the outer edge of the forearm.
description: Along the outer edge of the forearm.
function: Flexes the elbow, most strongly when the forearm is in a neutral (thumb up) position.
origin: Upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the radial styloid process.
actions: Flexes the elbow, most strongly when the forearm is in a neutral (thumb up) position.
clinicalRelevance: The brachioradialis reflex tests C5 and C6. It is often spared in radial nerve injuries at the arm.

name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
location: Back of the forearm on the thumb side.
description: Back of the forearm on the thumb side.
function: Extends and abducts the wrist.
origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
insertion: Dorsal base of the second metacarpal bone.
actions: Extends and abducts the wrist.
bloodSupply: Radial artery and radial recurrent artery.
clinicalRelevance: Radial nerve palsy causes wrist drop because the wrist extensors lose their supply.

name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
location: Back of the forearm, next to the long radial extensor.
description: Back of the forearm, next to the long radial extensor.
function: Extends and abducts the wrist and steadies it during gripping.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon).
insertion: Dorsal base of the third metacarpal bone.
actions: Extends and abducts the wrist and steadies it during gripping.
clinicalRelevance: The commonest site of tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis).

name: Extensor digitorum
location: Back of the forearm, the main finger extensor.
description: Back of the forearm, the main finger extensor.
function: Extends the fingers and the wrist.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon).
insertion: Extensor expansions of the four fingers, ending on the middle and distal phalanges.
actions: Extends the fingers and the wrist.
clinicalRelevance: Rupture of the extensor tendon over the finger causes a drooping fingertip ("mallet finger").

name: Extensor digiti minimi
location: Back of the forearm on the little finger side.
description: Back of the forearm on the little finger side.
function: Extends the little finger.
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon).
insertion: Extensor expansion of the little finger.
actions: Extends the little finger.
clinicalRelevance: It lets the little finger extend on its own.

name: Supinator
location: Deep, wrapping around the upper radius.
description: Deep, wrapping around the upper radius.
function: Turns the forearm so the palm faces up (supination).
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, the radial collateral ligament and the supinator crest of the ulna.
insertion: Upper third of the lateral, front and back surfaces of the radius.
actions: Turns the forearm so the palm faces up (supination).
bloodSupply: Radial recurrent and posterior interosseous arteries.
clinicalRelevance: The posterior interosseous nerve passes through it (arcade of Frohse). Compression there causes weak finger extension without sensory loss.

name: Abductor pollicis longus
location: Back of the forearm, emerging near the wrist on the thumb side.
description: Back of the forearm, emerging near the wrist on the thumb side.
function: Abducts and extends the thumb.
origin: Back of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane.
insertion: Base of the first metacarpal bone.
actions: Abducts and extends the thumb.
clinicalRelevance: With extensor pollicis brevis it forms the radial border of the anatomical snuffbox. De Quervain tenosynovitis affects both tendons.

name: Extensor pollicis brevis
location: Back of the forearm, running beside abductor pollicis longus.
description: Back of the forearm, running beside abductor pollicis longus.
function: Extends the first joint of the thumb.
origin: Back of the radius and interosseous membrane.
insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
actions: Extends the first joint of the thumb.
clinicalRelevance: Involved in De Quervain tenosynovitis (pain at the thumb side of the wrist).

name: Extensor pollicis longus
location: Back of the forearm; its tendon forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
description: Back of the forearm; its tendon forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
function: Extends the tip of the thumb and helps abduct the wrist.
origin: Middle third of the back of the ulna and the interosseous membrane.
insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb.
actions: Extends the tip of the thumb and helps abduct the wrist.
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon can rupture after a wrist fracture, making it hard to lift the thumb.

name: Extensor indicis
location: Deep back of the forearm.
description: Deep back of the forearm.
function: Extends the index finger independently (as in pointing).
origin: Back of the ulna and interosseous membrane.
insertion: Extensor expansion of the index finger.
actions: Extends the index finger independently (as in pointing).
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon is often used for tendon transfers.

name: Abductor pollicis brevis
location: Thenar eminence (thumb base).
description: Thenar eminence (thumb base).
function: Abducts the thumb away from the palm.
origin: Flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium.
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
innervation: Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Abducts the thumb away from the palm.
bloodSupply: Superficial palmar arch and radial artery.
clinicalRelevance: Wasting of the thenar eminence is seen in severe carpal tunnel syndrome.

name: Opponens pollicis
location: Deep in the thenar eminence.
description: Deep in the thenar eminence.
function: Brings the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips.
origin: Flexor retinaculum and trapezium.
insertion: Lateral half of the front of the first metacarpal.
innervation: Recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Brings the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips.
clinicalRelevance: Loss of opposition is a key sign of median nerve injury at the wrist.

name: Flexor pollicis brevis
location: Thenar eminence.
description: Thenar eminence.
function: Flexes the knuckle joint of the thumb.
origin: Flexor retinaculum and trapezium (superficial head); trapezoid and capitate (deep head).
insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
innervation: Superficial head: median nerve. Deep head: ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Flexes the knuckle joint of the thumb.
clinicalRelevance: A dual nerve supply explains why thumb flexion is partly kept after one nerve injury.

name: Adductor pollicis
location: Deep in the web between thumb and index finger.
description: Deep in the web between thumb and index finger.
function: Adducts the thumb towards the palm and gives pinch strength.
origin: Oblique head: capitate and bases of the second and third metacarpals. Transverse head: third metacarpal shaft.
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Adducts the thumb towards the palm and gives pinch strength.
clinicalRelevance: In ulnar nerve palsy the thumb flexes to compensate when pinching a sheet of paper (Froment sign).

name: Abductor digiti minimi (hand)
location: Hypothenar eminence (the pad below the little finger).
description: Hypothenar eminence (the pad below the little finger).
function: Abducts the little finger.
origin: Pisiform bone and the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Abducts the little finger.
bloodSupply: Ulnar artery and superficial palmar arch.
clinicalRelevance: Wasting of the hypothenar eminence points to an ulnar nerve lesion.

name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis (hand)
latinName: Musculus flexor digiti minimi brevis manus
location: Hypothenar eminence.
description: Hypothenar eminence.
function: Flexes the knuckle of the little finger.
origin: Hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum.
insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Flexes the knuckle of the little finger.
clinicalRelevance: Weak in ulnar nerve injury.

name: Opponens digiti minimi (hand)
location: Deep in the hypothenar eminence.
description: Deep in the hypothenar eminence.
function: Draws the fifth metacarpal forward to cup the palm.
origin: Hook of the hamate and flexor retinaculum.
insertion: Medial border of the fifth metacarpal.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Draws the fifth metacarpal forward to cup the palm.
clinicalRelevance: Weak in ulnar nerve injury (loss of cupping the palm).

name: Lumbricals of the hand
location: Four small muscles in the palm, arising from the flexor tendons.
description: Four small muscles in the palm, arising from the flexor tendons.
function: Flex the knuckles and extend the finger joints at the same time.
origin: Tendons of flexor digitorum profundus in the palm.
insertion: Extensor expansions on the back of the four fingers.
innervation: First and second: median nerve. Third and fourth: deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
actions: Flex the knuckles and extend the finger joints at the same time.
clinicalRelevance: In a claw hand (ulnar nerve palsy) the ring and little fingers are bent because the medial lumbricals are lost.

name: Dorsal interossei of the hand
location: Four muscles between the metacarpal bones.
description: Four muscles between the metacarpal bones.
function: Spread the fingers (abduction) and flex the knuckles.
origin: Adjacent sides of two metacarpal bones each (two heads).
insertion: Extensor expansions and bases of the proximal phalanges of the index, middle and ring fingers.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (T1).
actions: Spread the fingers (abduction) and flex the knuckles.
bloodSupply: Deep palmar arch and dorsal metacarpal arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Wasting between the metacarpals is seen in ulnar nerve palsy and in diseases of the anterior horn cells.

name: Palmar interossei of the hand
location: Three small muscles on the palm side between the metacarpals.
description: Three small muscles on the palm side between the metacarpals.
function: Bring the fingers together (adduction).
origin: Palmar sides of the second, fourth and fifth metacarpals.
insertion: Extensor expansions of the same fingers.
innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (T1).
actions: Bring the fingers together (adduction).
clinicalRelevance: Loss weakens finger adduction, which can be tested by gripping a card between the fingers.

name: Gluteus maximus
location: The largest and most superficial muscle of the buttock.
description: The largest and most superficial muscle of the buttock.
function: Extends and rotates the thigh outward at the hip. It is used for climbing stairs, running and getting up from sitting.
origin: Gluteal surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the sacrum and coccyx, and the sacrotuberous ligament.
insertion: Gluteal tuberosity of the femur (deep fibres) and the iliotibial tract (superficial fibres).
actions: Extends and rotates the thigh outward at the hip. It is used for climbing stairs, running and getting up from sitting.
clinicalRelevance: Injury of the inferior gluteal nerve causes difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. It is a common site for deep injections only in its upper outer part.

name: Gluteus medius
location: Outer surface of the hip, deep to gluteus maximus.
description: Outer surface of the hip, deep to gluteus maximus.
function: Abducts the thigh and holds the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
origin: Outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines.
insertion: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
actions: Abducts the thigh and holds the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
clinicalRelevance: Weakness causes the pelvis to drop on the opposite side when walking (positive Trendelenburg sign).

name: Gluteus minimus
location: Deepest of the three gluteal muscles.
description: Deepest of the three gluteal muscles.
function: Abducts and rotates the thigh inward; helps keep the pelvis level.
origin: Outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines.
insertion: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
actions: Abducts and rotates the thigh inward; helps keep the pelvis level.
clinicalRelevance: Works with gluteus medius; both are involved in greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

name: Tensor fasciae latae
location: Upper outer thigh, in front of the hip.
description: Upper outer thigh, in front of the hip.
function: Tenses the iliotibial tract, flexes and abducts the thigh and steadies the knee.
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the outer lip of the iliac crest.
insertion: Iliotibial tract, which ends on the lateral condyle of the tibia.
actions: Tenses the iliotibial tract, flexes and abducts the thigh and steadies the knee.
bloodSupply: Superior gluteal artery and lateral circumflex femoral artery.
clinicalRelevance: A tight iliotibial tract is linked to lateral knee pain in runners (iliotibial band syndrome).

name: Piriformis
location: Deep buttock, running from the sacrum to the greater trochanter.
description: Deep buttock, running from the sacrum to the greater trochanter.
function: Rotates the thigh outward when the hip is extended and abducts it when the hip is flexed.
origin: Front of the sacrum (S2 to S4) and the sacrotuberous ligament.
insertion: Upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur.
actions: Rotates the thigh outward when the hip is extended and abducts it when the hip is flexed.
clinicalRelevance: The sciatic nerve passes close to it, below it in most people. Spasm may compress the nerve (piriformis syndrome).

name: Obturator internus
location: Inside the pelvis, turning around the lesser sciatic notch to the hip.
description: Inside the pelvis, turning around the lesser sciatic notch to the hip.
function: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip joint.
origin: Inner surface of the obturator membrane and the surrounding pubis and ischium.
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
actions: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip joint.
clinicalRelevance: Forms part of the side wall of the pelvis and the ischioanal fossa.

name: Obturator externus
location: Deep, at the front and inner side of the hip.
description: Deep, at the front and inner side of the hip.
function: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip.
origin: Outer surface of the obturator membrane and the pubic and ischial rami.
insertion: Trochanteric fossa of the femur.
actions: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip.
bloodSupply: Obturator and medial circumflex femoral arteries.
clinicalRelevance: The medial circumflex artery lies beside it and supplies the femoral head.

name: Gemellus superior
location: Small muscle above the obturator internus tendon.
description: Small muscle above the obturator internus tendon.
function: Rotates the thigh outward.
origin: Ischial spine.
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter with the obturator internus tendon.
actions: Rotates the thigh outward.
clinicalRelevance: Part of the group of small outward rotators deep to gluteus maximus.

name: Gemellus inferior
location: Small muscle below the obturator internus tendon.
description: Small muscle below the obturator internus tendon.
function: Rotates the thigh outward.
origin: Ischial tuberosity.
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter with the obturator internus tendon.
innervation: Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1).
actions: Rotates the thigh outward.
clinicalRelevance: Part of the group of small outward rotators.

name: Quadratus femoris
location: Deep, below the gemelli, at the back of the hip.
description: Deep, below the gemelli, at the back of the hip.
function: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip joint.
origin: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity.
insertion: Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur.
innervation: Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1).
actions: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip joint.
clinicalRelevance: The medial circumflex artery runs deep to it and is at risk in hip fractures.

name: Iliacus
location: Inside the pelvis, lining the iliac fossa.
description: Inside the pelvis, lining the iliac fossa.
function: Flexes the thigh at the hip (with psoas major) and steadies the trunk.
origin: Iliac fossa and the ala of the sacrum.
insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur, joining the tendon of psoas major.
actions: Flexes the thigh at the hip (with psoas major) and steadies the trunk.
bloodSupply: Iliolumbar artery and deep circumflex iliac artery.
clinicalRelevance: An iliacus abscess or bleed can compress the femoral nerve.

name: Psoas major
location: Along the side of the lumbar spine, passing over the pelvic brim.
description: Along the side of the lumbar spine, passing over the pelvic brim.
function: Flexes the thigh at the hip and bends the lumbar spine sideways.
origin: Sides of the bodies of T12 to L5 and their discs, and the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae.
insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur.
innervation: Ventral rami of L1 to L3 (lumbar plexus).
actions: Flexes the thigh at the hip and bends the lumbar spine sideways.
bloodSupply: Lumbar branches of the abdominal aorta and iliolumbar artery.
clinicalRelevance: A tuberculous abscess of the spine can track down the sheath of psoas to the groin. Pain on extending the hip suggests psoas irritation (as in appendicitis).

name: Sartorius
location: The longest muscle, crossing the front of the thigh diagonally.
description: The longest muscle, crossing the front of the thigh diagonally.
function: Flexes, abducts and rotates the thigh outward and flexes the knee, as in sitting cross-legged.
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine.
insertion: Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
actions: Flexes, abducts and rotates the thigh outward and flexes the knee, as in sitting cross-legged.
clinicalRelevance: Forms the roof of the adductor canal and the lateral border of the femoral triangle.

name: Vastus lateralis
location: Outer front of the thigh, the largest part of quadriceps.
description: Outer front of the thigh, the largest part of quadriceps.
function: Extends the knee.
origin: Greater trochanter, the intertrochanteric line and the lateral lip of the linea aspera.
insertion: Base and lateral border of the patella, then the tibial tuberosity.
actions: Extends the knee.
clinicalRelevance: A common site for intramuscular injections in infants.

name: Vastus medialis
location: Inner front of the thigh, with its fibres running low towards the knee.
description: Inner front of the thigh, with its fibres running low towards the knee.
function: Extends the knee and keeps the patella from sliding outward.
origin: Intertrochanteric line, the spiral line and the medial lip of the linea aspera.
insertion: Medial border of the patella, then the tibial tuberosity.
actions: Extends the knee and keeps the patella from sliding outward.
clinicalRelevance: Weakness of its lower fibres is linked to kneecap pain and patellar instability.

name: Vastus intermedius
location: Deep to rectus femoris, on the front of the femur.
description: Deep to rectus femoris, on the front of the femur.
function: Extends the knee.
origin: Front and sides of the upper two-thirds of the femoral shaft.
insertion: Base of the patella, then the tibial tuberosity.
actions: Extends the knee.
clinicalRelevance: The quadriceps tendon formed with the other three parts is tested by the knee-jerk reflex (L3, L4).

name: Pectineus
location: Upper inner thigh, forming part of the floor of the femoral triangle.
description: Upper inner thigh, forming part of the floor of the femoral triangle.
function: Flexes and adducts the thigh.
origin: Pecten pubis (superior ramus of the pubis).
insertion: Pectineal line of the femur, behind the lesser trochanter.
innervation: Femoral nerve (L2, L3) and often the obturator nerve.
actions: Flexes and adducts the thigh.
bloodSupply: Medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries.
clinicalRelevance: A groin strain can involve it. Its nerve supply from two nerves is a classic exam point.

name: Adductor longus
location: Inner thigh, the most superficial adductor.
description: Inner thigh, the most superficial adductor.
function: Adducts the thigh.
origin: Front of the pubis, below the pubic crest.
insertion: Middle third of the linea aspera of the femur.
actions: Adducts the thigh.
clinicalRelevance: The most commonly strained muscle in a groin pull ("gracilis and adductor strains" in footballers).

name: Adductor brevis
location: Inner thigh, deep to pectineus and adductor longus.
description: Inner thigh, deep to pectineus and adductor longus.
function: Adducts the thigh and helps flex it.
origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
insertion: Upper part of the linea aspera and the pectineal line of the femur.
actions: Adducts the thigh and helps flex it.
clinicalRelevance: Separates the anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve.

name: Adductor magnus
location: The largest muscle of the inner thigh.
description: The largest muscle of the inner thigh.
function: Adducts the thigh; the hamstring part extends the hip.
origin: Inferior ramus of the pubis, ramus of the ischium and the ischial tuberosity.
insertion: Gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and the adductor tubercle of the femur.
innervation: Obturator nerve (adductor part) and the tibial part of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part), L2 to L4.
actions: Adducts the thigh; the hamstring part extends the hip.
bloodSupply: Deep femoral artery and obturator artery.
clinicalRelevance: Its adductor hiatus lets the femoral vessels pass to the back of the knee.

name: Gracilis
location: The long, thin muscle on the inner side of the thigh.
description: The long, thin muscle on the inner side of the thigh.
function: Adducts the thigh and flexes and rotates the leg inward at the knee.
origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
insertion: Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
actions: Adducts the thigh and flexes and rotates the leg inward at the knee.
clinicalRelevance: Often used as a flap in reconstruction and for transfers in hand and pelvic surgery.

name: Semitendinosus
location: Back of the thigh, a hamstring muscle with a long tendon.
description: Back of the thigh, a hamstring muscle with a long tendon.
function: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; rotates the leg inward.
origin: Ischial tuberosity.
insertion: Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
innervation: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2).
actions: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; rotates the leg inward.
bloodSupply: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery.
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon is a graft source for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

name: Semimembranosus
location: Back of the thigh, deep to semitendinosus.
description: Back of the thigh, deep to semitendinosus.
function: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; rotates the leg inward.
origin: Ischial tuberosity.
insertion: Posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle.
innervation: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2).
actions: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; rotates the leg inward.
bloodSupply: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery.
clinicalRelevance: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee (Baker cyst) often arises between its tendon and the gastrocnemius.

name: Biceps femoris
location: Outer back of the thigh, a hamstring muscle.
description: Outer back of the thigh, a hamstring muscle.
function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip; rotates the leg outward.
origin: Long head: ischial tuberosity. Short head: lateral lip of the linea aspera.
insertion: Head of the fibula and the lateral condyle of the tibia.
innervation: Long head: tibial part of the sciatic nerve. Short head: common fibular part (L5, S1, S2).
actions: Flexes the knee and extends the hip; rotates the leg outward.
bloodSupply: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery.
clinicalRelevance: The common fibular nerve runs along its tendon. Hamstring strains are common in sprinters.

name: Soleus
location: Deep to gastrocnemius in the calf.
description: Deep to gastrocnemius in the calf.
function: Plantar-flexes the foot. It is vital for standing and walking, and acts as a "peripheral heart" by pumping venous blood up the leg.
origin: Back of the head and upper shaft of the fibula, and the soleal line of the tibia.

name: Plantaris
location: Thin muscle between gastrocnemius and soleus.
description: Thin muscle between gastrocnemius and soleus.

origin: Lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
insertion: Calcaneus, medial to the calcaneal tendon.
actions: Weakly assists plantar flexion and knee flexion.
clinicalRelevance: Its long tendon can be mistaken for a nerve and is used as a graft.

name: Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
location: Back of the ankle, the thickest tendon of the body.
description: Back of the ankle, the thickest tendon of the body.

insertion: Back of the calcaneus (heel bone).

clinicalRelevance: Rupture is common in middle-aged athletes. A positive Thompson test (no foot movement when the calf is squeezed) confirms it.

name: Popliteus
location: Behind the knee, deep.
description: Behind the knee, deep.
