origin: Lateral condyle of the femur and the lateral meniscus.
insertion: Posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line.
actions: Unlocks the knee at the start of flexion by rotating the femur outward on the tibia.
bloodSupply: Inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Injury is linked to posterolateral corner damage of the knee.

name: Tibialis anterior
location: Front of the leg, beside the shin.
description: Front of the leg, beside the shin.
function: Dorsiflexes the foot and inverts it.
origin: Upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia and the interosseous membrane.
insertion: Medial cuneiform bone and the base of the first metatarsal.
actions: Dorsiflexes the foot and inverts it.
clinicalRelevance: Weakness causes foot drop. Shin splints often involve this muscle.

name: Tibialis posterior
location: Deep back of the leg.
description: Deep back of the leg.
function: Inverts the foot and plantar-flexes it; supports the medial arch.
origin: Interosseous membrane and the back of the tibia and fibula.
insertion: Navicular tuberosity and most of the tarsal bones.
actions: Inverts the foot and plantar-flexes it; supports the medial arch.
clinicalRelevance: Tendon dysfunction leads to an acquired flat foot.

name: Extensor digitorum longus
location: Front and outer leg.
description: Front and outer leg.
function: Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.
origin: Lateral condyle of the tibia, upper fibula and interosseous membrane.
insertion: Middle and distal phalanges of the four lateral toes.
actions: Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.
clinicalRelevance: Compartment syndrome of the front of the leg can ischaemically damage it.

name: Extensor hallucis longus
location: Front of the leg, between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus.
description: Front of the leg, between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus.
function: Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the foot.
origin: Middle of the front of the fibula and the interosseous membrane.
insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the big toe.
actions: Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the foot.
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon is a landmark for the dorsalis pedis pulse.

name: Fibularis longus
location: Outer leg.
description: Outer leg.
function: Everts the foot and plantar-flexes it; supports the arches.
origin: Head and upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula.
insertion: Medial cuneiform bone and base of the first metatarsal.
actions: Everts the foot and plantar-flexes it; supports the arches.
clinicalRelevance: Common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck weakens eversion and dorsiflexion.

name: Fibularis brevis
location: Outer leg, deep to fibularis longus.
description: Outer leg, deep to fibularis longus.
function: Everts the foot and weakly plantar-flexes it.
origin: Lower two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula.
insertion: Tuberosity of the base of the fifth metatarsal.
actions: Everts the foot and weakly plantar-flexes it.
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon can be injured in ankle sprains; avulsion fracture of the fifth metatarsal base occurs with sudden inversion.

name: Fibularis tertius
location: Front and outer lower leg, part of extensor digitorum longus.
description: Front and outer lower leg, part of extensor digitorum longus.
function: Dorsiflexes and everts the foot.
origin: Distal third of the front of the fibula.
insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the fifth metatarsal.
actions: Dorsiflexes and everts the foot.
clinicalRelevance: Absent in about 10 per cent of people.

name: Flexor digitorum longus
location: Deep back of the leg, inner side.
description: Deep back of the leg, inner side.
function: Flexes the toes and helps plantar-flex the foot.
origin: Medial part of the back of the tibia below the soleal line.
insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of the four lateral toes.
actions: Flexes the toes and helps plantar-flex the foot.
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel.

name: Flexor hallucis longus
location: Deep back of the leg, outer side.
description: Deep back of the leg, outer side.
function: Flexes the big toe and gives the main push-off in walking.
origin: Lower two-thirds of the back of the fibula.
insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the big toe.
actions: Flexes the big toe and gives the main push-off in walking.
clinicalRelevance: Tenosynovitis is common in dancers.

name: Extensor digitorum brevis
location: Top of the foot, in front of the ankle.
description: Top of the foot, in front of the ankle.
function: Extends the toes.
origin: Upper and lateral surface of the calcaneus.
insertion: Extensor expansions of the first to fourth toes (the part to the big toe is extensor hallucis brevis).
actions: Extends the toes.
clinicalRelevance: Swelling over the sinus tarsi should not be mistaken for a lump; the muscle can bruise in ankle sprains.

name: Abductor hallucis
location: Inner edge of the sole.
description: Inner edge of the sole.
function: Abducts and flexes the big toe; supports the medial arch.
origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and flexor retinaculum.
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe.
actions: Abducts and flexes the big toe; supports the medial arch.
clinicalRelevance: Tight or weak muscle is linked to a bunion (hallux valgus).

name: Flexor digitorum brevis
location: Middle of the sole, just under the plantar aponeurosis.
description: Middle of the sole, just under the plantar aponeurosis.
function: Flexes the middle joints of the lateral four toes and supports the arch.
origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis.
insertion: Sides of the middle phalanges of the four lateral toes.
actions: Flexes the middle joints of the lateral four toes and supports the arch.
clinicalRelevance: Plantar fasciitis pain at the heel arises close to its origin.

name: Abductor digiti minimi (foot)
location: Outer edge of the sole.
description: Outer edge of the sole.
function: Abducts and flexes the little toe.
origin: Medial and lateral processes of the calcaneal tuberosity.
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little toe.
actions: Abducts and flexes the little toe.
clinicalRelevance: Can be compressed in tight shoes.

name: Quadratus plantae (flexor accessorius)
location: Deep in the sole.
description: Deep in the sole.
function: Straightens the pull of flexor digitorum longus so the toes flex directly.
origin: Medial and lateral surfaces of the calcaneus.
insertion: Tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
actions: Straightens the pull of flexor digitorum longus so the toes flex directly.
clinicalRelevance: Weakness gives a less effective grip of the toes.

name: Flexor hallucis brevis
location: Under the first metatarsal.
description: Under the first metatarsal.
function: Flexes the big toe joint. The two sesamoid bones lie in its tendons.
origin: Cuboid and lateral cuneiform bones.
insertion: Both sides of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe.
actions: Flexes the big toe joint. The two sesamoid bones lie in its tendons.
clinicalRelevance: Sesamoiditis causes pain under the ball of the big toe.

name: Adductor hallucis
location: Deep in the forefoot of the sole.
description: Deep in the forefoot of the sole.
function: Adducts the big toe and supports the transverse arch.
origin: Oblique head: bases of the second to fourth metatarsals. Transverse head: plantar ligaments of the third to fifth toes.
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe.
actions: Adducts the big toe and supports the transverse arch.
bloodSupply: Lateral plantar artery and plantar arch.
clinicalRelevance: Helps hold the big toe against hallux valgus drift.

name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis (foot)
latinName: Musculus flexor digiti minimi brevis pedis
location: Outer sole, beside the fifth metatarsal.
description: Outer sole, beside the fifth metatarsal.
function: Flexes the little toe.
origin: Base of the fifth metatarsal and the long plantar ligament.
insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the little toe.
actions: Flexes the little toe.
clinicalRelevance: Small, with little clinical importance on its own.

name: Lumbricals of the foot
location: Four small muscles in the sole.
description: Four small muscles in the sole.
function: Flex the toe knuckles and extend the toe tips.
origin: Tendons of flexor digitorum longus.
insertion: Extensor expansions on the first four toes.
innervation: First: medial plantar nerve. Others: lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3).
actions: Flex the toe knuckles and extend the toe tips.
clinicalRelevance: Wasting contributes to clawing of the toes in neuropathy.

name: Dorsal interossei of the foot
location: Between the metatarsal bones.
description: Between the metatarsal bones.
function: Spread the toes and flex the toe knuckles.
origin: Adjacent sides of two metatarsal bones each.
insertion: Extensor expansions and proximal phalanges of the second to fourth toes.
actions: Spread the toes and flex the toe knuckles.
clinicalRelevance: Weakness gives claw toes in diabetic neuropathy.

name: External oblique
location: Side and front of the abdomen, the most superficial lateral muscle.
description: Side and front of the abdomen, the most superficial lateral muscle.
function: Flexes and twists the trunk to the opposite side, and compresses the abdomen.
origin: Outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs.
insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle and the anterior half of the iliac crest.
innervation: Ventral rami of T7 to T12 and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
actions: Flexes and twists the trunk to the opposite side, and compresses the abdomen.
bloodSupply: Lower posterior intercostal, subcostal and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament. Weakness at the groin allows inguinal hernia.

name: Internal oblique
location: Deep to the external oblique on the side of the abdomen.
description: Deep to the external oblique on the side of the abdomen.
function: Flexes and twists the trunk to the same side and compresses the abdomen.
origin: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the lateral inguinal ligament.
insertion: Lower three or four ribs, linea alba and pubic crest (conjoint tendon).
innervation: Ventral rami of T7 to L1, including the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
actions: Flexes and twists the trunk to the same side and compresses the abdomen.
bloodSupply: Deep circumflex iliac and inferior epigastric arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Its lower fibres form the conjoint tendon and the roof of the inguinal canal.

name: Transversus abdominis
location: Deepest layer of the side abdominal wall.
description: Deepest layer of the side abdominal wall.
function: Compresses the abdomen and stabilises the lower back.
origin: Inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and inguinal ligament.
insertion: Linea alba and pubic crest.
innervation: Ventral rami of T7 to L1.
actions: Compresses the abdomen and stabilises the lower back.
bloodSupply: Deep circumflex iliac and inferior epigastric arteries.
clinicalRelevance: The "core" stabiliser. The TAP block anaesthetises nerves in the plane in front of it.

name: Quadratus lumborum
location: Back wall of the abdomen, beside the lumbar spine.
description: Back wall of the abdomen, beside the lumbar spine.
function: Bends the trunk sideways and fixes the twelfth rib in breathing.
origin: Iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament.
insertion: Twelfth rib and the transverse processes of L1 to L4.
innervation: Ventral rami of T12 to L4.
actions: Bends the trunk sideways and fixes the twelfth rib in breathing.
clinicalRelevance: A common source of low back pain. The kidneys lie in front of it.

name: Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis)
location: Long columns on both sides of the spine.
description: Long columns on both sides of the spine.
function: Extends and straightens the spine and bends it sideways.
origin: Sacrum, iliac crest and spinous processes of the lumbar vertebrae (common tendon).
insertion: Ribs, transverse and spinous processes and the skull base (mastoid process).
actions: Extends and straightens the spine and bends it sideways.
clinicalRelevance: Strain gives the commonest form of low back pain. Spasm is felt as a tight band beside the spine.

name: Multifidus
location: Deep muscle along the spine, in the groove between spinous and transverse processes.
description: Deep muscle along the spine, in the groove between spinous and transverse processes.
function: Stabilises the spine and extends and rotates it slightly.
origin: Sacrum, lumbar mammillary processes and thoracic transverse processes.
insertion: Spinous processes of the vertebrae two to four levels higher.
actions: Stabilises the spine and extends and rotates it slightly.
bloodSupply: Dorsal branches of the segmental arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Wasting is linked to chronic low back pain.

name: Semispinalis
location: Deep muscle of the back of the neck and upper back.
description: Deep muscle of the back of the neck and upper back.
function: Extends and rotates the head and spine.
origin: Transverse processes of C4 to T12.
insertion: Occipital bone and spinous processes of the vertebrae above.
innervation: Dorsal rami of cervical and thoracic nerves.
actions: Extends and rotates the head and spine.
clinicalRelevance: Weak in whiplash-type neck pain.

name: Splenius capitis and cervicis
location: Back of the neck, under trapezius.
description: Back of the neck, under trapezius.
function: Extends and rotates the head and neck.
origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T6.
insertion: Mastoid process and the transverse processes of C1 to C3.
actions: Extends and rotates the head and neck.
clinicalRelevance: Tension here causes neck stiffness and headache.

name: Serratus posterior superior
location: Upper back, deep to the rhomboids.
description: Upper back, deep to the rhomboids.
function: Raises the ribs slightly in inspiration.
origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T3.
insertion: Upper borders of ribs 2 to 5.
innervation: Ventral rami of T1 to T4.
actions: Raises the ribs slightly in inspiration.
clinicalRelevance: A minor accessory muscle of breathing.

name: Serratus posterior inferior
location: Lower back, deep to latissimus dorsi.
description: Lower back, deep to latissimus dorsi.
function: Pulls the lower ribs down and back in expiration.
origin: Spinous processes of T11 to L2.
insertion: Lower borders of ribs 9 to 12.
innervation: Ventral rami of T9 to T12.
actions: Pulls the lower ribs down and back in expiration.
clinicalRelevance: A minor muscle of breathing.

name: Transversus thoracis
location: Inner surface of the front chest wall.
description: Inner surface of the front chest wall.
function: Depresses the costal cartilages in expiration.
origin: Back of the lower sternum and xiphoid process.
insertion: Inner surfaces of costal cartilages 2 to 6.
actions: Depresses the costal cartilages in expiration.
clinicalRelevance: Lies behind the sternum; the internal thoracic vessels run in front of it.

name: Sternocleidomastoid
location: Side of the neck, running from behind the ear to the collarbone.
description: Side of the neck, running from behind the ear to the collarbone.
function: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side; both together flex the neck.
origin: Manubrium of the sternum and the medial third of the clavicle.
insertion: Mastoid process and the lateral superior nuchal line.
innervation: Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) and cervical nerves C2, C3.
actions: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side; both together flex the neck.
clinicalRelevance: Congenital torticollis comes from shortening or fibrosis of this muscle in infants. Accessory nerve injury causes weakness.

name: Scalene muscles
location: Side of the neck, from the cervical spine to the first two ribs.
description: Side of the neck, from the cervical spine to the first two ribs.
function: Raise the first and second ribs in breathing and bend the neck sideways.
origin: Transverse processes of C2 to C7.
insertion: First rib (anterior and middle scalenes) and second rib (posterior scalene).
innervation: Ventral rami of C3 to C8.
actions: Raise the first and second ribs in breathing and bend the neck sideways.
bloodSupply: Ascending cervical and transverse cervical arteries.
clinicalRelevance: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes. Compression here causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

name: Platysma
location: Thin sheet just under the skin of the neck.
description: Thin sheet just under the skin of the neck.
function: Tightens the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth down.
origin: Fascia over the upper chest and shoulder.
insertion: Lower border of the mandible and the skin of the lower face.
innervation: Cervical branch of the facial nerve.
actions: Tightens the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth down.
clinicalRelevance: Facial nerve palsy can cause loss of its tension.

name: Subclavius
location: Small muscle under the clavicle.
description: Small muscle under the clavicle.
function: Draws the clavicle down and steadies the sternoclavicular joint.
origin: First rib and its costal cartilage.
insertion: Groove on the underside of the clavicle.
actions: Draws the clavicle down and steadies the sternoclavicular joint.
clinicalRelevance: Lies in front of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels and protects them in clavicle fractures.

name: Longus colli
location: Front of the cervical spine.
description: Front of the cervical spine.
function: Flexes the neck.
origin: Bodies of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae.
insertion: Atlas and bodies of the upper cervical vertebrae.
innervation: Ventral rami of C2 to C6.
actions: Flexes the neck.
bloodSupply: Inferior thyroid and ascending pharyngeal arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Injury (whiplash) can swell the retropharyngeal space.

name: Longus capitis
location: Front of the upper cervical spine.
description: Front of the upper cervical spine.
function: Flexes the head and neck.
origin: Transverse processes of C3 to C6.
insertion: Basilar part of the occipital bone.
innervation: Ventral rami of C1 to C3.
actions: Flexes the head and neck.
clinicalRelevance: A deep neck flexor weakened in neck pain.

name: Masseter
location: Side of the cheek, over the angle of the jaw.
description: Side of the cheek, over the angle of the jaw.
function: Closes the jaw and clenches the teeth.
origin: Zygomatic arch.
insertion: Lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible.
innervation: Mandibular nerve (V3) through the masseteric nerve.
actions: Closes the jaw and clenches the teeth.
bloodSupply: Masseteric branch of the maxillary artery and facial artery.
clinicalRelevance: Enlarged by teeth grinding (bruxism). Pain here is common in temporomandibular joint disorders.

name: Temporalis
location: Side of the head, in the temporal fossa.
description: Side of the head, in the temporal fossa.
function: Closes the jaw; the posterior fibres retract the jaw.
origin: Temporal fossa and the temporal fascia.
insertion: Coronoid process and the anterior border of the ramus of the mandible.
innervation: Deep temporal branches of the mandibular nerve (V3).
actions: Closes the jaw; the posterior fibres retract the jaw.
clinicalRelevance: Pain in the temple can mean tension headache; temporal arteritis affects the artery above it.

name: Medial pterygoid
location: Deep to the ramus of the mandible.
description: Deep to the ramus of the mandible.
function: Closes the jaw and moves it sideways.
origin: Medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the pyramidal process of the palatine bone.
insertion: Medial surface of the angle of the mandible.
innervation: Medial pterygoid nerve from the mandibular nerve (V3).
actions: Closes the jaw and moves it sideways.
bloodSupply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
clinicalRelevance: Spasm limits jaw opening (trismus) after a wisdom tooth operation.

name: Lateral pterygoid
location: Deep in the infratemporal fossa.
description: Deep in the infratemporal fossa.
function: Opens the jaw by pulling the mandible forward and moves it side to side.
origin: Upper head: infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid. Lower head: lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.
insertion: Neck of the mandible and the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint.
innervation: Lateral pterygoid nerve from the mandibular nerve (V3).
actions: Opens the jaw by pulling the mandible forward and moves it side to side.
bloodSupply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
clinicalRelevance: Dysfunction contributes to clicking of the jaw joint.

name: Digastric
location: Below the jaw, two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon at the hyoid.
description: Below the jaw, two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon at the hyoid.
function: Opens the jaw and raises the hyoid in swallowing.
origin: Anterior belly: digastric fossa of the mandible. Posterior belly: mastoid notch.
insertion: Intermediate tendon attached to the hyoid bone.
innervation: Anterior belly: nerve to mylohyoid (V3). Posterior belly: facial nerve.
actions: Opens the jaw and raises the hyoid in swallowing.
clinicalRelevance: Landmark that divides the neck into triangles.

name: Mylohyoid
location: Floor of the mouth.
description: Floor of the mouth.
function: Raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid in swallowing.
origin: Mylohyoid line of the mandible.
insertion: Hyoid bone and median raphe.
actions: Raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid in swallowing.
clinicalRelevance: Forms the muscular floor of the mouth; infection spreads above or below it in Ludwig angina.

name: Geniohyoid
location: Above the mylohyoid in the floor of the mouth.
description: Above the mylohyoid in the floor of the mouth.
function: Pulls the hyoid forward and up.
origin: Inferior mental spine of the mandible.
insertion: Body of the hyoid bone.
innervation: C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve.
actions: Pulls the hyoid forward and up.
clinicalRelevance: Helps open the jaw and keeps the airway open in sleep.

name: Stylohyoid
location: Runs along the digastric from the skull to the hyoid.
description: Runs along the digastric from the skull to the hyoid.
function: Pulls the hyoid up and back in swallowing.
origin: Styloid process of the temporal bone.
insertion: Body of the hyoid bone.
actions: Pulls the hyoid up and back in swallowing.
clinicalRelevance: An elongated styloid process can cause throat pain (Eagle syndrome).

name: Omohyoid
location: Side of the neck, from the shoulder blade to the hyoid.
description: Side of the neck, from the shoulder blade to the hyoid.
function: Depresses and steadies the hyoid.
origin: Superior border of the scapula.
insertion: Lower border of the hyoid bone.
actions: Depresses and steadies the hyoid.
clinicalRelevance: Landmark that divides the posterior triangle of the neck.

name: Sternohyoid
location: Front of the neck, over the thyroid gland.
description: Front of the neck, over the thyroid gland.
function: Depresses the hyoid after swallowing.
origin: Manubrium and the medial end of the clavicle.
insertion: Lower border of the hyoid bone.
actions: Depresses the hyoid after swallowing.
clinicalRelevance: One of the "strap muscles" divided in thyroid surgery.

name: Sternothyroid
location: Front of the neck, deep to sternohyoid.
description: Front of the neck, deep to sternohyoid.
function: Pulls the larynx down.
origin: Back of the manubrium.
insertion: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
actions: Pulls the larynx down.
clinicalRelevance: Lies directly in front of the thyroid gland.

name: Thyrohyoid
location: Front of the neck, above the thyroid cartilage.
description: Front of the neck, above the thyroid cartilage.
function: Raises the larynx and lowers the hyoid.
origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
insertion: Greater horn and body of the hyoid bone.
innervation: C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve.
actions: Raises the larynx and lowers the hyoid.
clinicalRelevance: Helps close the airway in swallowing.

name: Buccinator
location: The muscle of the cheek.
description: The muscle of the cheek.
function: Presses the cheek against the teeth in chewing and blowing.
origin: Outer surfaces of the maxilla and mandible near the molars, and the pterygomandibular raphe.
insertion: Orbicularis oris and the angle of the mouth.
innervation: Buccal branches of the facial nerve.
actions: Presses the cheek against the teeth in chewing and blowing.
clinicalRelevance: Facial palsy lets food collect in the cheek.

name: Levator ani and coccygeus
location: Floor of the pelvis, forming a sling.
description: Floor of the pelvis, forming a sling.
function: Supports the pelvic organs and keeps urinary and faecal continence.
origin: Pubic bone, tendinous arch of levator ani and ischial spine.
insertion: Perineal body, anococcygeal ligament and coccyx.
innervation: Nerve to levator ani (S3, S4) and the pudendal nerve.
actions: Supports the pelvic organs and keeps urinary and faecal continence.
bloodSupply: Inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries.
clinicalRelevance: Childbirth can damage it, leading to prolapse and stress incontinence.

name: Bones of the hand
location: Distal to the forearm bones.
description: Eight carpal bones in two rows (scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate), five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges.
function: Form the wrist, palm and fingers; give attachment to the forearm and hand muscles.
clinicalRelevance: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone (fall on an outstretched hand) and may heal poorly because of its blood supply. A boxer's fracture affects the fifth metacarpal neck.

name: Bones of the foot
location: Distal to the leg bones.
description: Seven tarsal bones (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms), five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges.
function: Form the arches of the foot and give attachment to the leg and foot muscles.
clinicalRelevance: Stress fractures of the metatarsals are common in runners. A fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal follows sudden inversion of the ankle.

name: Patellar ligament
location: Front of the knee, between the kneecap and the shin bone.
description: A strong flat white band that is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon below the patella.
function: Transmits the pull of the quadriceps to the tibia, so the knee can straighten. It is tapped with a hammer in the knee-jerk reflex (L3, L4).
origin: Apex (lower tip) of the patella.
insertion: Tibial tuberosity.
clinicalRelevance: Rupture or tendinopathy ("jumper's knee") weakens or stops straightening of the knee. Surgeons often use its central third as a graft to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament.

name: Medial collateral ligament of the knee
location: Inner side of the knee.
description: A broad flat band on the inner side of the knee that blends with the medial meniscus.
function: Stops the knee from bending inward (valgus stress) and steadies it when it is straight.
origin: Medial epicondyle of the femur.
insertion: Medial surface of the upper tibial shaft.
clinicalRelevance: The most commonly injured knee ligament, usually from a blow to the outer side of the knee (a tackle). The terrible triad is a tear of this ligament, the anterior cruciate and the medial meniscus.

name: Lateral collateral ligament of the knee
location: Outer side of the knee.
description: A rounded cord on the outer side of the knee. It is separate from the joint capsule and the lateral meniscus.
function: Stops the knee from bending outward (varus stress).
origin: Lateral epicondyle of the femur.
insertion: Head of the fibula.
clinicalRelevance: Injured by a blow to the inner side of the knee or by twisting. The common fibular nerve runs close behind it and may be hurt in the same injury.

name: Anterior cruciate ligament
location: Inside the knee joint, in the middle between the femur and the tibia.
description: A strong band that runs from the back of the femur forward and down to the front of the tibia. Schematic position.
function: Stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur and controls twisting. It is a main stabiliser of the knee.
origin: Inner side of the lateral femoral condyle (back part).
insertion: Front of the intercondylar area of the tibia.
clinicalRelevance: Tears are common in sports with sudden stops, jumps or side-steps (football, basketball, skiing). The knee feels unstable and a positive Lachman or anterior drawer test is found. Reconstruction uses a graft.

name: Posterior cruciate ligament
location: Inside the knee joint, crossing behind the anterior cruciate.
description: A thick band that runs from the front of the femoral notch backward and down to the back of the tibia. Schematic position.
function: Stops the tibia from sliding backward on the femur. It is stronger than the anterior cruciate.
origin: Outer surface of the medial femoral condyle.
insertion: Back of the intercondylar area of the tibia.
clinicalRelevance: Torn in a hard blow to the front of the shin (a dashboard injury in a car crash) or by overextension. The tibia sags backward (posterior drawer sign).

name: Iliotibial tract
location: Outer side of the thigh, from the hip to below the knee.
description: A thick white band of deep fascia (a long flat tendon) that receives the tensor fasciae latae and most of gluteus maximus.
function: Steadies the hip and knee when standing and walking and helps hold the knee straight.
origin: Iliac crest and the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus.
insertion: Lateral condyle of the tibia (Gerdy's tubercle).
clinicalRelevance: Iliotibial band syndrome, a common cause of outer knee pain in runners and cyclists, comes from friction over the lateral femoral epicondyle.

name: Inguinal ligament
location: Crease between the lower abdomen and the thigh.
description: A band formed by the lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis. It runs between the hip bone and the pubis.
function: Forms the floor of the inguinal canal and the roof of the passage to the thigh for the femoral vessels and nerve.
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine.
insertion: Pubic tubercle.
clinicalRelevance: Inguinal hernias push through the inguinal canal above this ligament; femoral hernias come through below it. It is the landmark for locating the femoral artery (mid-inguinal point) and nerve.

name: Linea alba
location: Vertical midline of the abdomen, from the breastbone to the pubis.
description: A tough white line formed where the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles meet between the two rectus abdominis muscles.
function: Joins the right and left sides of the abdominal wall and gives attachment to the abdominal muscles. It has few blood vessels, which makes it a favourite surgical incision.
origin: Xiphoid process and costal margin.
insertion: Pubic symphysis.
clinicalRelevance: A midline incision through the linea alba opens the abdomen with little bleeding. Weak spots cause midline hernias (epigastric hernia, incisional hernia). Pregnancy can widen it (diastasis recti).

name: Flexor retinaculum of the wrist
location: Front of the wrist, over the carpal bones.
description: A thick white band that bridges the curve of the carpal bones and turns it into the carpal tunnel.
function: Holds the finger flexor tendons close to the wrist and forms the roof of the carpal tunnel through which the median nerve passes.
origin: Pisiform and hook of the hamate.
insertion: Scaphoid tubercle and trapezium.
clinicalRelevance: Carpal tunnel syndrome: swelling in the tunnel squeezes the median nerve, causing numbness and tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers and weak grip. Treatment can include cutting this ligament.

name: Interosseous membrane of the forearm
location: Between the radius and the ulna.
description: A strong white fibrous sheet that joins the shafts of the two forearm bones.
function: Transfers force from the hand (radius) to the ulna and the arm, and gives attachment to deep forearm muscles.
origin: Interosseous border of the radius.
insertion: Interosseous border of the ulna.
clinicalRelevance: If a fall on the outstretched hand fractures the radius, the force passes along this sheet. A tear with a radial head fracture and wrist injury is called an Essex-Lopresti injury.

name: Interosseous membrane of the leg
location: Between the tibia and the fibula.
description: A strong white fibrous sheet joining the shafts of the two leg bones. It has an opening at the top for the anterior tibial vessels.
function: Binds the leg bones together, passes weight from the tibia to the fibula and gives attachment to deep leg muscles.
origin: Interosseous border of the tibia.
insertion: Interosseous border of the fibula.
clinicalRelevance: Tears in high ankle sprains (syndesmosis injuries) and in tibia and fibula fractures can leave the ankle unstable.

name: Long plantar ligament
location: Sole of the foot, along the outer side.
description: The longest white ligament of the foot. It runs from the heel bone to the cuboid and the base of the outer metatarsals.
function: Helps hold up the long arch of the foot and bridges the tendon of fibularis longus.
origin: Plantar surface of the calcaneus.
insertion: Cuboid and bases of metatarsals 2 to 5.
clinicalRelevance: Overstretching helps cause flat foot (fallen arch) and heel and midfoot pain.

name: Duodenum
location: Upper abdomen, a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas.
description: The first and shortest part of the small intestine (about 25 cm). It receives acid food from the stomach, bile from the gallbladder and enzymes from the pancreas.
function: Neutralises stomach acid, mixes food with bile and pancreatic juice and starts the absorption of iron and calcium.
clinicalRelevance: Duodenal ulcers are common and are mostly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or anti-inflammatory drugs. A bleeding ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery. A tumour of the head of the pancreas can block the duodenal loop or the bile duct.

name: Jejunum
location: Upper left part of the middle abdomen.
description: The middle part of the small intestine (about 2.5 m). Its wall has tall circular folds, so it looks feathery inside and has a rich blood supply.
function: The main site of absorption of sugars, amino acids, fats and vitamins.
clinicalRelevance: Coeliac disease flattens the folds of the jejunum and causes poor absorption. Crohn disease may inflame it. Removing a long segment can cause short bowel syndrome.

name: Ileum
location: Lower right part of the middle abdomen, ending at the caecum.
description: The last and longest part of the small intestine (about 3.5 m). It has Peyer patches (lymphoid tissue) and ends at the ileocaecal valve.
function: Absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts and the last of the nutrients, and keeps back large bowel bacteria through the ileocaecal valve.
clinicalRelevance: Crohn disease commonly affects the terminal ileum. A Meckel diverticulum is a leftover pouch 60 cm before the end that can bleed or inflame like appendicitis. Removal of the ileum causes vitamin B12 deficiency.

name: Appendix
location: Lower right abdomen, attached to the caecum just below the ileocaecal valve.
description: A narrow blind-ended tube about 9 cm long with a lot of lymphoid tissue in its wall. Its tip can lie in several positions.
function: Probably helps immune defence and may store helpful gut bacteria.
clinicalRelevance: Appendicitis begins with vague central abdominal pain that moves to the lower right (McBurney point) with fever and vomiting. It needs urgent assessment because a burst appendix causes peritonitis.

name: Costal cartilages
location: Between the front ends of the ribs and the breastbone.
description: Bars of hyaline cartilage that join the upper seven ribs to the sternum. They are drawn here in pale blue-white.
function: Make the chest wall springy, so the ribs can move for breathing and absorb blows.
clinicalRelevance: Costochondritis (inflamed cartilage joints) causes chest wall pain that is tender to touch. Cartilage turns to bone with age, making the chest stiffer. They can fracture in CPR.

name: Intervertebral discs
location: Between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae, from the second cervical vertebra to the sacrum.
description: Pads with a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) around a soft gel centre (nucleus pulposus). They make up about a quarter of the length of the spine.
function: Absorb shocks, allow bending and twisting and keep the gaps for the spinal nerves open.
clinicalRelevance: A slipped (herniated) disc pushes the gel through the ring, most often at L4-L5 or L5-S1, and presses on a nerve root, causing sciatica (pain down the leg) or numbness. Discs dry out and thin with age.

name: Mandible
location: The lower jaw, hinged to the temporal bone just in front of the ear.
description: The only movable bone of the skull. A horizontal body carries the lower teeth; two vertical rami end in the condyle (joint) and the coronoid process (muscle attachment). The mental foramen and the mandibular canal carry the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels.
function: Chewing, speech, and opening and closing the mouth at the temporomandibular joint. Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) attach to it.
clinicalRelevance: Fractures are often double (for example the body and the opposite angle) and the teeth show whether the bite is shifted. Dislocation of the temporomandibular joint locks the mouth open. The inferior alveolar nerve can be injured in wisdom tooth surgery, causing numbness of the lower lip.

name: Teeth
location: Set in the upper jaw (maxilla) and the lower jaw (mandible).
description: An adult has 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars. Each tooth has an enamel-covered crown, a root in the bony socket and a pulp cavity with nerves and vessels inside dentine.
function: Bite, cut and grind food, help speech and shape the face.
clinicalRelevance: Dental caries (decay) is the commonest disease worldwide. Untreated, it spreads to the pulp and causes abscess. Gum disease (periodontitis) loosens teeth. Impacted wisdom teeth are common reasons for surgery.

name: Hyoid bone
location: In the front of the neck at the level of C3, above the thyroid cartilage, below the mandible.
description: A small U-shaped bone that does not join any other bone; it is held by muscles and ligaments. It has a body and greater and lesser horns.
function: Anchors the tongue and the muscles of the floor of the mouth and the larynx, and moves up during swallowing.
clinicalRelevance: A fractured hyoid in an adult is a classic sign of strangulation. It is very rarely injured otherwise.

name: Renal artery
location: From the abdominal aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery to the kidney hilum.
description: A large paired artery. The right one passes behind the inferior vena cava. Each divides into segmental arteries inside the kidney.
function: Supplies the kidney with about a fifth of the output of the heart for filtering blood.
clinicalRelevance: Narrowing (renal artery stenosis) causes hard-to-treat high blood pressure. A blocked or torn artery can destroy the kidney. In kidney donation the artery is cut and joined to the recipient vessels.

name: Renal vein
location: From the kidney hilum to the inferior vena cava.
description: The left vein is longer and passes in front of the aorta; it also receives the left gonadal and adrenal veins.
function: Drains filtered blood from the kidney into the inferior vena cava.
clinicalRelevance: A kidney cancer can grow into the renal vein and along the vena cava. A left varicocele may occur because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Coeliac trunk and branches
location: Arises from the aorta at the level of T12, just under the diaphragm.
description: A short trunk that splits into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. They are drawn together here.
function: Supplies the foregut: the lower oesophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas and the upper duodenum.
clinicalRelevance: A bleeding gastric ulcer may involve the left gastric artery. A splenic artery aneurysm can rupture in pregnancy. Compression by the diaphragm can cause median arcuate ligament syndrome with pain after eating.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superior mesenteric artery
location: Arises from the aorta at L1, behind the pancreas, and runs down in the root of the mesentery.
description: Supplies the midgut: the lower duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and most of the transverse colon.
function: Carries blood to most of the small bowel and the right colon.
clinicalRelevance: Sudden blockage (an embolus) causes severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the findings. This is a surgical emergency, as the bowel dies within hours (mesenteric ischaemia).

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Inferior mesenteric artery
location: Arises from the aorta at L3 and runs down on the left.
description: Supplies the hindgut: the left third of the transverse colon, the descending and sigmoid colon and the upper rectum.
function: Carries blood to the left colon and upper rectum.
clinicalRelevance: It is tied during surgery for aortic aneurysm or colon cancer. The left colon near the splenic flexure is vulnerable to ischaemic colitis because the supply from two arteries meets there.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Superior mesenteric vein
location: Runs beside the superior mesenteric artery on its right side.
description: Drains the small intestine, caecum, ascending colon and transverse colon, and joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
function: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver.
clinicalRelevance: Thrombosis of this vein causes bowel congestion and pain. A pancreatic cancer can grow around it and make it impossible to remove.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Splenic vein
location: Runs from the spleen along the back of the pancreas.
description: Collects blood from the spleen, the stomach and the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
function: Drains the spleen and part of the stomach and pancreas towards the liver.
clinicalRelevance: In pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer the splenic vein can clot, causing sectoral (left-sided) portal hypertension with gastric varices.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Internal iliac artery
location: Runs from the division of the common iliac artery down into the pelvis.
description: Supplies the pelvic organs, the gluteal muscles, the inner thigh and the perineum through its anterior and posterior divisions.
function: Carries blood to the bladder, rectum, uterus or prostate, the gluteal region and the genitals.
clinicalRelevance: Tied or blocked to stop severe bleeding after childbirth or pelvic fracture. In men, narrowing can cause erectile problems and buttock pain on walking.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: External iliac artery
location: Runs along the pelvic brim from the common iliac division to the inguinal ligament.
description: Becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament. It gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches.
function: Carries the main blood supply to the leg.
clinicalRelevance: Atherosclerosis here causes pain in the thigh and buttock when walking (claudication). It is the artery used for leg access in some heart and aorta procedures.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Iliac veins
location: Beside the matching iliac arteries; the two common iliac veins join to form the inferior vena cava at L5.
description: The external, internal and common iliac veins collect blood from the leg and pelvis.
function: Return blood from the pelvic organs and the leg to the inferior vena cava.
clinicalRelevance: The left common iliac vein is crossed by the right common iliac artery, and compression there (May-Thurner syndrome) can cause left leg deep vein thrombosis.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Subclavian artery
location: Arches over the first rib behind the collarbone.
description: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left directly from the aortic arch. It gives off the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk and becomes the axillary artery.
function: Supplies the arm, the neck, part of the brain (through the vertebral artery) and the chest wall.
clinicalRelevance: Blockage before the vertebral artery branch can steal blood from the brain when the arm is used (subclavian steal syndrome), causing dizziness. It can be compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Subclavian and brachiocephalic veins
location: Behind the collarbone and into the upper chest, joining to form the superior vena cava.
description: The subclavian veins drain the arms and join the internal jugular veins to form the brachiocephalic veins, which unite as the superior vena cava.
function: Return blood from the arms, head and neck to the right atrium.
clinicalRelevance: A popular site for central venous catheters. Clots after catheters or in thoracic outlet syndrome cause an arm that is swollen and blue.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Internal jugular vein
location: Runs down the side of the neck beside the common carotid artery in the carotid sheath.
description: The main vein of the head and neck. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus and joins the subclavian vein.
function: Drains the brain, face and neck.
clinicalRelevance: The jugular venous pressure (JVP) is read from its pulsation in the neck and shows heart failure. It is a common route for central venous lines.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Axillary artery
location: Armpit (axilla), from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major.
description: The continuation of the subclavian artery. It lies behind pectoralis minor and is wrapped by the cords of the brachial plexus.
function: Carries oxygen-rich blood to the shoulder, chest wall and arm. It becomes the brachial artery.
clinicalRelevance: A shoulder dislocation or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus can injure it and the axillary nerve. Its branches link around the shoulder blade, so blood can still reach the arm if the main vessel is blocked slowly.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Radial artery
location: Outer (thumb) side of the front of the forearm, then the wrist and the back of the hand.
description: One of the two end branches of the brachial artery. It runs under brachioradialis and lies just under the skin at the wrist.
function: Supplies the outer forearm, the thumb side of the hand and (with the ulnar artery) the deep palmar arch.
clinicalRelevance: The pulse is felt here at the wrist. It is the usual site for arterial blood gas samples and for a catheter in heart procedures. Before it is used, the Allen test shows that the ulnar artery can supply the hand.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Ulnar artery
location: Inner (little finger) side of the front of the forearm, then the palm.
description: The larger end branch of the brachial artery. It runs deep to the flexor muscles, then beside the ulnar nerve to the wrist and forms the superficial palmar arch.
function: Supplies the inner forearm and most of the palm and fingers through the superficial palmar arch.
clinicalRelevance: A cut at the wrist often injures the ulnar artery together with the ulnar nerve and the tendons. Damage to the palmar arch (for example in a deep cut of the palm) causes heavy bleeding that must be controlled from both the radial and ulnar sides.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Popliteal artery
location: Back of the knee (popliteal fossa).
description: The continuation of the femoral artery after it passes through the adductor hiatus. It lies deepest in the fossa, next to the femur and the knee capsule, and divides below the knee.
function: Supplies the knee joint and the muscles around it, then divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
clinicalRelevance: A knee dislocation or a fracture of the lower femur can tear or block it, which threatens the leg within hours. A popliteal aneurysm is the commonest peripheral aneurysm and is found as a throbbing swelling behind the knee. The pulse is felt with the knee bent.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Anterior tibial artery
location: Front of the leg, on the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula.
description: Arises below the knee, passes forward through the top of the interosseous membrane and runs down the front of the leg with the deep fibular nerve. At the ankle it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery.
function: Supplies the muscles of the front of the leg (the extensor compartment) and the top of the foot.
clinicalRelevance: The dorsalis pedis pulse on the top of the foot is checked to assess blood flow in peripheral arterial disease. Swelling in the front compartment of the leg (compartment syndrome) can squeeze this artery and the deep fibular nerve and cause foot drop.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Posterior tibial artery
location: Back of the leg, deep to soleus, then behind the inner ankle bone.
description: The larger end branch of the popliteal artery. It runs with the tibial nerve down the back of the leg and divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries in the sole.
function: Supplies the calf muscles and the sole of the foot. It gives off the fibular (peroneal) artery.
clinicalRelevance: The pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus. Absent pulses with cold, painful feet suggest peripheral arterial disease; this is common in people who smoke or have diabetes.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Axillary vein
location: Armpit, in front of and below the axillary artery.
description: Formed where the basilic vein joins the brachial veins. It becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
function: Drains blood from the arm and the upper chest wall back towards the heart.
clinicalRelevance: Deep vein thrombosis here (for example after a pacemaker wire or a central line, or from hard repeated arm effort) causes a swollen, bluish arm.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Cephalic vein
location: Just under the skin on the thumb (outer) side of the forearm and the outer side of the upper arm.
description: A long superficial vein that runs in the groove between deltoid and pectoralis major and drains into the axillary vein.
function: Drains the outer side of the hand, forearm and arm.
clinicalRelevance: Often used for drips and blood tests, and for a fistula for kidney dialysis. Cutting down on it at the shoulder gives access to the venous system.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Basilic vein
location: Just under the skin on the little finger (inner) side of the forearm. In the arm it dives deep to join the brachial veins.
description: A long superficial vein on the inner side of the arm. Above the elbow it passes through the deep fascia to form the axillary vein with the brachial veins.
function: Drains the inner side of the hand and forearm.
clinicalRelevance: A common site for drawing blood and placing a PICC line. The median cubital vein, which links it to the cephalic vein at the elbow, is the usual place for venepuncture; the median nerve and brachial artery lie deep to it.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Femoral vein
location: Front and inner side of the thigh, beside the femoral artery.
description: The continuation of the popliteal vein. It lies on the inner side of the femoral artery in the femoral triangle and becomes the external iliac vein behind the inguinal ligament.
function: Drains blood from the deep structures of the leg and thigh.
clinicalRelevance: A common site of deep vein thrombosis, which causes a swollen, painful leg and may send a clot to the lungs (pulmonary embolism). It is the vein used for access in many heart and venous procedures.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Great saphenous vein
location: Just under the skin along the inner side of the leg and thigh, from the inner ankle to the groin.
description: The longest vein in the body. It starts at the inner side of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus, ascends the inner leg and thigh and joins the femoral vein at the saphenous opening.
function: Drains the skin and superficial tissues of the leg. It lies near the saphenous nerve.
clinicalRelevance: Varicose veins form when its valves fail. Segments are harvested for coronary bypass grafts. A cut-down at the ankle gives emergency venous access.

sources.locator: Chapter 20: The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation

name: Median nerve
location: Runs down the middle of the front of the arm and forearm, then through the carpal tunnel into the palm.
description: Formed from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus (C5 to T1). It lies beside the brachial artery in the arm, passes between the two heads of pronator teres and runs between the superficial and deep finger flexors.
function: Supplies most of the forearm flexors, the thenar muscles (thumb) and the first two lumbricals. Gives sensation to the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger on the palm side.
clinicalRelevance: Carpal tunnel syndrome (compression under the flexor retinaculum) causes numbness and tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers and weak thumb movement. A high lesion gives the "hand of benediction" when the person tries to make a fist. It can be injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus.

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Ulnar nerve
location: Inner side of the arm, behind the medial epicondyle (the funny bone), then along the inner forearm to the little finger side of the hand.
description: A branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8, T1). It passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and enters the hand beside the pisiform.
function: Supplies flexor carpi ulnaris, half of flexor digitorum profundus, most small hand muscles and the skin of the little finger and half of the ring finger.
clinicalRelevance: Hitting the elbow ("funny bone") gives tingling in the little finger. Cubital tunnel syndrome and injury cause a claw hand, weak grip and loss of finger spreading (Froment sign).

sources.locator: Chapter 13: Anatomy of the Nervous System

name: Saphenous nerve
location: Inner side of the thigh, knee, leg and foot, with the great saphenous vein.
description: The longest branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs in the adductor canal and then beside the great saphenous vein.
function: Gives sensation to the skin of the inner side of the leg and foot.
clinicalRelevance: It can be injured in saphenous vein surgery or knee operations and cause numbness or burning along the inner leg. It is blocked in the adductor canal for knee surgery pain relief.
